META.subtitleDoc: CBE Phenomenon-Driven Lesson Sequence — Sub-Strand 1.3 (10 Lessons)

UNIT.subject: Chemistry
UNIT.content:
• Development of the periodic table (Groups and periods)
• Ion formation (oxidation number, valency, radicals)
• Formulae and chemical equations
• Chemical families: alkali metals, alkaline earth metals, halogens, noble gases and transition elements
UNIT.learningOutcomes:
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) relate the position of an element in the periodic table to its electron arrangement,
b) illustrate ion formation of elements,
c) derive the formulae of compounds,
d) write balanced equations for chemical reactions,
e) appreciate the role of electron arrangement in the development of the periodic table.
UNIT.coreCompetencies:
• Communication and Collaboration: the learner listens keenly and actively using open questions while discussing with peers the relationship between atomic number, mass number and number of electrons in atoms of elements.
• Critical thinking and problem solving: the learner creates new ideas while drawing diagrams of ions of selected elements using dots and/or crosses to illustrate ion formation.
• Learning to learn: the learner learns independently by writing balanced equations for chemical reactions.
• Citizenship: the learner appreciates contributions made by various scientists on the development of atomic structure and the periodic table.
UNIT.values: • Peace: The learner shows compassion as they display tolerance while predicting the type of ion formed from the electron arrangement of elements with peers.
UNIT.sep:
• Developing and using models: learners build and revise a cumulative model linking electron arrangement to position, ion formation and formulae.
• Analyzing and interpreting data: learners examine element card data (atomic number, electron arrangement, reactivity) to find patterns in groups and periods.
• Planning and carrying out investigations: learners test the reactivity of selected elements, e.g. observing sodium, calcium and magnesium behaviour via demonstrations or simulations.
• Using mathematics and computational thinking: learners balance equations and derive formulae using valencies and oxidation numbers.
• Constructing explanations: learners explain why elements in the same group behave similarly.
UNIT.pcis:
• Socio-Economic and Environmental Issues (social cohesion): as the learner discusses with peers how atoms acquire stability.
• Life skills (analytical thinking): as the learner predicts the type of ion formed from a given electron arrangement of an atom.
UNIT.careers:
• Chemist or analytical chemist at KEBS or the Kenya Bureau of Standards: uses periodic trends to test product quality.
• Water treatment engineer (e.g. Nairobi City Water): uses chlorine and fluorine compounds.
• Agronomist or soil scientist (Kericho, Rift Valley): selects potassium and nitrogen fertilizers.
• Pharmacist or medical laboratory technologist: selects compounds for treatments.
• Materials and battery engineer: uses sodium and lithium compounds.
UNIT.focus: Learners investigate how electron arrangement determines an element's position in the periodic table and its chemical family. They then use this to predict ion formation, valency and oxidation numbers, derive formulae and write balanced equations. The unit follows a phenomenon-driven storyline with predict, observe, explain, Driving Question Board and model-building phases in each lesson.
UNIT.phenomenon: How does electron arrangement influence the arrangement of elements in the periodic table? Learners receive a set of element cards (the first 20 elements) showing symbol, atomic number and properties, but not their positions. They are asked to sort them as chemists did before they knew about electrons. They then observe that elements such as sodium, potassium and lithium (used in batteries and found in Kenyan fertilizers like potassium compounds) react vigorously with water, while neon and argon do not react at all, and that chlorine and fluorine compounds are used in water treatment in Kenyan towns such as Nairobi and Mombasa. It is puzzling that elements with very different masses behave alike and fall into the same column, while neighbouring elements behave very differently. What hidden property of atoms creates these patterns and lets chemists predict the ions and compounds of elements they have never worked with?
UNIT.supportingPhenomena:
• Why potassium and nitrogen fertilizers suit particular soils in the Rift Valley and Kericho tea farms, while sodium and calcium compounds behave differently.
• Why chlorine and fluorine compounds are used in water treatment plants in Kenyan towns, and why both are in the same family.
• Why lithium and sodium are used in batteries and react in similar ways with water.
• Why neon and argon in lighting and welding do not form compounds, yet sodium and chlorine combine to make table salt (sodium chloride) used in ugali and sukuma wiki cooking.
UNIT.drivingQuestion:
DRIVING QUESTION: How does electron arrangement influence the arrangement of elements in the periodic table, and how does it help us predict the ions and compounds elements form?

KICD KEY INQUIRY QUESTIONS:
1. The KICD curriculum design excerpt supplied for sub-strand 1.3 does not list a key inquiry question; the sub-strand is guided by the teacher's phenomenon question: How does electron arrangement influence the arrangement of elements in the periodic table?
2. (The key inquiry question shown in the excerpt, 'How do chemical bonds influence the properties of substances?', belongs to Sub-Strand 1.4 Chemical Bonding and is the forward link from this unit.)
UNIT.storylineThread:
Lesson 1: Students sort element cards of the first 20 elements and brainstorm how scientists such as Mendeleev and Moseley arranged them; the DQB is launched with the phenomenon.
Lesson 2: Development of the periodic table: groups, periods and the role of atomic number; students arrange the first 20 elements into groups and periods.
Lesson 3: Writing electron arrangements (s and p notation) and relating them to group and period number.
Lesson 4: Chemical families: alkali metals, alkaline earth metals, halogens, noble gases and transition elements; reactivity patterns observed through demonstration or simulation.
Lesson 5: Stability of atoms: why atoms lose or gain electrons; the noble gas stable arrangement.
Lesson 6: Ion formation: predicting cations and anions from electron arrangements and drawing dot-and-cross diagrams; electron arrangement of ions.
Lesson 7: Valency and oxidation numbers inferred from electron arrangement; elements with variable oxidation numbers (e.g. iron, copper).
Lesson 8: Radicals and deriving formulae of compounds using valencies and oxidation numbers, e.g. NaCl, CaCl2, Al2O3, and fertilizer compounds such as KNO3.
Lesson 9: Writing and balancing chemical equations for simple reactions, e.g. sodium with water.
Lesson 10: Final model revision and presentation: students use electron arrangement to explain the phenomenon, predict an unfamiliar element's position, ion and formula, and link forward to chemical bonding.

LESSONS.title: Sorting the Element Cards and Launching the DQB
LESSONS.duration: 40 minutes (one lesson of the 30 lessons in Sub-Strand 1.3)
LESSONS.aresKeywords: element cards, atomic number, relative atomic mass, pattern, group, alkali metals, noble gases, reactivity, Mendeleev, Moseley, Driving Question Board, phenomenon

slo.purpose: To launch the phenomenon: why do elements with very different masses behave alike and sit in the same column, while neighbouring elements behave very differently? Learners sort the first 20 element cards the way early chemists did, discover that sorting by properties and mass reveals patterns but also leaves puzzles, and open the Driving Question Board (DQB).
slo.knowledge: Elements can be sorted by properties and by relative atomic mass (A_r) into patterns. Mass alone leaves puzzles: Li (A_r 7), Na (23) and K (39) are very different in mass yet all react vigorously with water, while neighbouring elements such as Na and Mg, or F and Ne, behave very differently. Ne and Ar do not react at all. Chlorine is used to disinfect water in Nairobi and Mombasa. Ar (A_r 40) is heavier than K (A_r 39) although Ar has the smaller atomic number (Z 18 against Z 19).
slo.skills: Sorting and classifying data (NGSS SEP: Analyzing and Interpreting Data); asking questions and defining problems (writing DQB questions); developing and using models (initial Class Model, the 'Electron Arrangement Model' poster); constructing explanations (initial ideas); communication and collaboration (listening keenly and using open questions in groups).
slo.attitudes: Curiosity about hidden patterns in matter; tolerance and compassion when peers' ideas differ (Peace); appreciation of the contributions of scientists such as Mendeleev and Moseley to the development of the periodic table (Citizenship); willingness to say 'I do not know yet' (Learning to learn).
slo.keyInquiry: How does electron arrangement influence the arrangement of elements in the periodic table, and how does it help us predict the ions and compounds elements form? (Teacher's phenomenon question; the KICD excerpt for 1.3 lists no key inquiry question. 'How do chemical bonds influence the properties of substances?' belongs to Sub-Strand 1.4 and is the forward link.)
slo.purposeInStoryline: This is the launch lesson and builds on nothing earlier except learners' prior knowledge of atoms from earlier grades (protons, neutrons, electrons). It raises the puzzles that later lessons resolve: Lesson 2 uses the Ar/K mass puzzle to introduce the history from Mendeleev to Moseley and the idea of groups and periods; Lesson 3 writes electron arrangements; Lesson 4 returns to the Li, Na, K observations. Lesson 1 does NOT explain why; it only creates the need to know.
slo.safetyNotes: This lesson uses cards, video or teacher description of reactions, and no learner handling of reactive metals. If Mwalimu Achieng demonstrates the water reactions, only a trained teacher may use a pea-sized piece of sodium or lithium, behind a safety screen, with goggles on, learners at least 2 m away, and a small amount of water in a large trough. Potassium must NOT be demonstrated in school; show it by video or description only. Never touch the metals with fingers; store them under oil. Chlorine gas must not be used; chlorine in water treatment is discussed from information only.

LESSONS.overview: Wanjiku, Otieno, Amina and Kipchoge's Grade 10 class in Kisumu receives envelopes of 20 Element Cards (symbol, atomic number Z, A_r and properties, but NOT position). Learners first predict how chemists, before they knew about electrons, would sort the cards, then sort them in groups, record their rules, and notice what works and what does not. Mwalimu Achieng then presents the phenomenon: Li, Na and K, with very different masses, all react vigorously with water, while Ne and Ar do not react at all; chlorine and fluorine compounds treat water in Nairobi and Mombasa; Ar (A_r 40) is heavier than K (A_r 39) but comes before it. Learners explain what they think is happening, launch the DQB with their questions, and draw an initial Class Model, the 'Electron Arrangement Model' poster, that is revised in every lesson.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners sit in groups of four. Mwalimu Achieng holds up a bag of maize, beans and a few mixed seeds (or draws them) and asks how they would sort them. Learners then see the envelope of 20 Element Cards (H to Ca) showing symbol, Z, A_r and a property, but no position. Individually, for 2 minutes, learners write in their notebooks: 'Before anyone knew about electrons, how might chemists have sorted these 20 elements? What would you use to put them in order and groups? What do you think will be difficult?' They then share with a partner. Each learner also writes a one-sentence prediction: 'I think elements like lithium, sodium and potassium will behave ___ when put in water because ___.'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Imagine you are a chemist in 1860. You know about mass and about what elements look like and do, but nothing about electrons. How would you organise 20 elements?' Hold up the maize and beans example and ask: 'How did you sort these? What feature did you choose?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before taking answers. Ask learners to write silently for 2 minutes. Circulate and note 3 different predictions. Cold-call 3 learners (for example Amina, Otieno, Kipchoge) to share a sorting idea and 2 learners to share their water prediction. Say: 'I am not looking for the right answer; I want your honest thinking.' Do not correct predictions. Record 4-5 predictions on the board under 'Our first ideas'.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Eliciting prior knowledge through individual prediction followed by think-pair-share. Writing before talking commits every learner to an idea so they can later see how their thinking changes, and linking sorting seeds to sorting elements connects familiar Kenyan food items to the unfamiliar task, building a bridge to the phenomenon.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) at least 80% of learners have written a sorting criterion (for example mass, colour, metal or non-metal, state) and a water prediction; (2) learners give reasons rather than just guesses; (3) note misconceptions such as 'heavier elements are more reactive' or 'all metals react the same'. Tally the sorting criteria suggested (mass, state, metallic or not) on the board to use in the next phase.

framework.learnerExperience: Part A (15 minutes): Groups spread out the 20 Element Cards and sort them in two rounds. Round 1: sort by properties (metal or non-metal, state, how it behaves). Round 2: arrange all 20 in a single line by increasing A_r, then try to make rows and columns of elements that behave alike. They record their rules on a group chart. Part B (10 minutes): Mwalimu Achieng presents evidence (video or safe teacher demonstration of lithium and sodium; description or video only for potassium): Li fizzes steadily and floats; Na melts into a ball, darts about and fizzes fast; K melts, burns with a lilac flame and reacts very vigorously. Learners compare with data cards showing that Ne and Ar do not react at all. They read short information on chlorine used to disinfect Lake Victoria water in Nairobi and Mombasa, and on fluoride compounds in some water supplies. In a table they record for each element: Z, A_r, behaviour with water.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute the envelopes and say: 'Your job is to find patterns. There is no single right way yet.' Give 5 minutes for sorting by properties, then say: 'Now put them in order of mass, from H (1) to Ca (40). Look for elements that behave alike. What do you notice?' Circulate and ask each group: 'Which cards did you struggle to place? Why?' Use WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after each question. For Part B, show the Li, Na and K reactions and ask: 'What is the same? What is different?' Pause the video after each metal and ask learners to turn and talk for 30 seconds. Then project the data table with Li 7, Na 23, K 39 and Ne 20, Ar 40 side by side and ask: 'Li, Na and K are very different in mass. What do you notice about how they behave?' Cold-call 3 groups. Then ask: 'Ne and Ar do not react at all. What do you notice about their masses and where they might sit?' Cold-call 2 learners. Point out that Ar (A_r 40) is heavier than K (A_r 39) and Ca (A_r 40) equals Ar in mass: ask 'If we line up by mass alone, where should Ar and K go?' Do not resolve the puzzle; say: 'Hold that thought; it will matter.' Safety: remind learners not to touch reactive metals; only the trained teacher handles them behind the screen.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Data sorting and pattern-seeking (Analyzing and Interpreting Data) with a Notice and Wonder routine. Learners physically manipulate cards to generate patterns, discover that the mass line works partly but breaks down, and use the 'notice' and 'wonder' structure to separate observation from explanation, which keeps the focus on evidence and creates real cognitive conflict about the hidden property.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observe whether groups: (1) produce at least one valid pattern (for example metals on the left, gases elsewhere, repeating reactivity); (2) correctly identify that Li, Na, K behave alike despite different masses; (3) notice that Ne and Ar are unreactive; (4) notice a placement difficulty for Ar and K. Look for use of data (Z, A_r) in group talk. A group that only says 'they are different' without citing numbers or behaviours needs a prompt: 'Which numbers show that?' Collect the group charts as evidence.

framework.learnerExperience: Groups discuss and write on their charts: 'What patterns did we find? What puzzles remain? What could be the hidden property of atoms that makes Li, Na and K alike but Na and Mg, or F and Ne, different?' Using their prior knowledge of atoms from earlier grades (protons, neutrons, electrons), they suggest initial explanations in sentence starters: 'I think ___ because ___.' Learners then take part in a short class discussion in which Wanjiku, Otieno, Amina and Kipchoge's group-style ideas are compared. Mwalimu Achieng briefly mentions that scientists such as Mendeleev and Moseley grappled with the same puzzle and asks learners to brainstorm in groups how they might have arranged the elements, without giving the answer. Each learner then writes a 2-3 sentence individual explanation in their notebook: 'What do you think makes elements behave alike?'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'We have two kinds of evidence: patterns that work and puzzles that do not fit. Let us talk about both.' Ask: 'What does sorting by mass explain? What does it NOT explain?' WAIT 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 4 learners from different groups, asking each to build on the previous answer ('Do you agree or disagree with Kipchoge? Why?'). Push thinking with: 'What might atoms have inside them that is the same in Li, Na and K, even though their masses differ?' Accept 'electrons' or 'protons' as hypotheses but do not confirm or reject: say 'Good idea. Hold it as a hypothesis; we will test it.' Mention in one minute that Mendeleev (Russian chemist, 1869) arranged elements by mass and left gaps, and that Moseley (English physicist, 1913) showed that atomic number is the true basis of order, but do not teach more here, since Lesson 2 develops this. Address misconceptions respectfully (for example 'heavier means more reactive') by referring back to the K, Na and Li data. Insist on peaceful, respectful listening: 'We disagree with ideas, not people.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-evidence-reasoning discussion with a talk move of 'build on, agree or disagree'. Learners must link claims to the specific data (Li 7, Na 23, K 39 all reactive; Ne, Ar unreactive; Ar 40 versus K 39) so that explanations are anchored in evidence, and they frame a testable hypothesis about a hidden atomic property, building an explanatory need for the lessons that follow.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check individual explanations for: (1) a claim that links to evidence (for example 'Li, Na, K react alike so something inside atoms must be the same'); (2) recognition that mass alone is not enough; (3) an initial hypothesis about electrons, protons or arrangement. Use a 3-level look-for: Level 1 describes only; Level 2 identifies a puzzle; Level 3 proposes a hidden property with a reason. Record the number of learners at each level on a class list to compare with the end of the unit.

framework.learnerExperience: Mwalimu Achieng reveals the Driving Question on a large wall chart: 'How does electron arrangement influence the arrangement of elements in the periodic table, and how does it help us predict the ions and compounds elements form?' Learners each write 2 questions on sticky notes, using the puzzles and observations from today (for example 'Why do Li, Na and K react alike when their masses are so different?', 'Why do neon and argon not react?', 'Why is chlorine used to treat water in Nairobi and Mombasa?', 'Why does argon come before potassium although it is heavier?', 'How can chemists predict what a new element will do?'). Groups combine and sort their notes into categories (for example 'patterns and groups', 'why some elements do not react', 'ions and formulae'), then post them on the DQB wall chart. The class chooses 2 or 3 questions to investigate first.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Good scientists ask questions. Write what you are still wondering after today. Questions that start with how or why are especially powerful.' Model one question and one improvement ('Why is sodium reactive?' becomes 'Why do sodium and potassium react alike even though they have different masses?'). Give 3 minutes of silent writing with WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before groups talk. Walk around and ask: 'Which of your questions connects to a puzzle we saw?' Cold-call 4 groups to read and place a question, asking them to explain where they put it and why. Cluster similar questions together on the board and name the clusters with learners. Say: 'We will return to this board in every lesson, move questions we can answer, and add new ones.' Keep the DQB visible and photograph or copy it for the offline record. Point out the link to the KICD sub-strand: 'This is the key to the whole unit, from how elements are arranged to the ions and formulae they form.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board (question-asking and clustering). Learners generate and categorise their own questions from evidence, which gives them ownership of the learning path, makes their curiosity visible, and gives a record against which growing understanding is tracked in later lessons.
framework.formativeAssessment: Count and review the sticky notes: look for at least 2 per learner; questions that refer to specific evidence (Li, Na, K; Ne, Ar; chlorine in Nairobi and Mombasa; Ar and K masses); and questions that ask how or why rather than yes or no. Note which learners ask about electrons or atomic structure. Use a quick check: ask 3 learners 'Which question on the board matters most to you and why?' Identify learners who wrote only factual or off-topic questions for gentle follow-up.

framework.learnerExperience: Groups draw their first version of the Class Model on a large sheet titled 'Electron Arrangement Model'. It shows: (1) the 20 elements as they placed them (a line or grid), (2) arrows for patterns that worked (for example Li, Na, K react alike), (3) question marks for puzzles (Ar and K; Ne and Ar unreactive), and (4) a labelled sketch of an atom with a nucleus and electrons showing 'hidden property?' as their initial idea of what decides behaviour. They add a short caption: 'What we think decides where an element belongs and how it behaves.' Groups do a short gallery walk (3 minutes) to compare models, and then the class agrees on a single starter version to be posted next to the DQB.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'A model is our best current idea, and it is meant to change. Show what you know and mark clearly what you do not know yet.' Provide sentence starters: 'We think ___ because ___. We are not sure about ___.' Walk around and ask: 'Where does mass show up in your model? Where does something else need to?' Allow WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 3 groups to explain one feature of their model during the gallery walk, and ask 2 other learners to say what they would add. Combine the ideas into one class poster, and say: 'We will revise this poster after each lesson. By Lesson 10 we should be able to use it to predict the position, ion and formula of an element we have never worked with.' Close with a quick exit ticket: 'Write one thing you are now sure of, and one thing you are still wondering.' Remind learners of the forward steps: in Lesson 2 we look at how Mendeleev and Moseley solved the ordering problem.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Initial model building with explicit uncertainty. Drawing a model that shows what is known, what is a question and what is a hidden mechanism forces learners to organise evidence and ideas into one representation (Developing and Using Models), and the model gives later lessons something concrete to revise instead of starting from nothing.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check each group model for: (1) the elements placed with some pattern shown; (2) at least one evidence-based pattern (Li, Na, K alike); (3) at least one puzzle marked (Ar and K, or Ne and Ar unreactive); (4) a hypothesis about a hidden property inside the atom. Use the exit tickets to sort learners into 'sure of a pattern', 'sure of a puzzle' and 'no clear idea', and plan targeted questions for Lesson 2. Look for respectful, tolerant discussion during the gallery walk.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect: (1) Did every learner offer a sorting rule and a prediction before seeing evidence? (2) Which patterns did groups find on their own, and which puzzles (Li, Na, K alike; Ar and K masses; Ne and Ar unreactive) did they spot without help? (3) Which misconceptions appeared (for example 'heavier means more reactive', 'all metals react alike') and how will you revisit them with evidence in Lessons 2 to 4? (4) Was wait time of 10-15 seconds used consistently, and did cold-calling include quieter learners? (5) Did the DQB capture questions about electrons, groups, ions and formulae, and which clusters are missing? (6) Were safety rules followed during the water reaction presentation? (7) Record the number of learners at each explanation level for comparison at the end of the unit. Keep the DQB, group charts and Class Model poster ready for Lesson 2.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We sorted the first 20 Element Cards (H to Ca) by properties and by mass. We saw that Li, Na and K, with very different masses (7, 23, 39), all react with water, with the reaction getting stronger from Li to K, while Ne and Ar do not react at all. We noted that chlorine is used to treat water in Nairobi and Mombasa, and that Ar (A_r 40) is heavier than K (A_r 39) although it comes first.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Elements can be sorted by properties and by mass into patterns, but mass alone does not explain why some elements of very different mass behave alike while neighbouring elements behave very differently. Mendeleev and Moseley faced this puzzle, and something hidden inside atoms must decide where an element belongs and how it behaves.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Our first ideas: a hidden property of atoms, possibly linked to electrons, may explain why Li, Na and K are alike and why Ne and Ar are unreactive. We do not yet know what it is. We started the DQB with the driving question and our own questions, and drew the first version of the Class Model, the 'Electron Arrangement Model', to be revised in each lesson.

LESSONS.title: From Mendeleev's Gaps to Moseley's Atomic Number: Building Groups and Periods
LESSONS.aresKeywords: periodic table, Mendeleev, Moseley, atomic number, group, period, atomic mass, element cards

slo.purpose: Learners trace how the periodic table was developed from Mendeleev (1869, ordered by atomic mass, left gaps) to Moseley (1913, atomic number), define groups (columns) and periods (rows), and arrange the first 20 elements by atomic number into groups and periods.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson the learner should be able to: (1) state that Mendeleev in 1869 ordered elements by atomic mass and left gaps for undiscovered elements; (2) state that Moseley in 1913 showed that atomic number is the true basis of order; (3) define a group as a vertical column and a period as a horizontal row; (4) arrange H to Ca by atomic number into groups 1 to 18 and periods 1 to 4, and explain why Ar (A_r 40) comes before K (A_r 39).
slo.skills: Developing and using models (arranging the Element Cards into a table); analysing and interpreting data (comparing Z and A_r columns); constructing explanations from evidence (why mass ordering fails for Ar and K); engaging in argument from evidence.
slo.attitudes: Learners appreciate the contributions of scientists such as Mendeleev and Moseley to the development of the periodic table (Citizenship). Learners show tolerance and listen respectfully when peers disagree about placement of cards (Peace). Learners practise analytical thinking (Life skills).
slo.keyInquiry: How does electron arrangement influence the arrangement of elements in the periodic table? (Today: what is the true basis of the order, and what do rows and columns mean?)
slo.purposeInStoryline: In Lesson 1, learners sorted the Element Cards by properties and mass and found that mass alone leaves puzzles: Li, Na and K behave alike, while neighbours behave very differently. Lesson 2 resolves part of the puzzle: elements are ordered by atomic number, and the table has columns (groups) and rows (periods). It does not yet explain WHY elements in a column behave alike. That question is carried to Lesson 3, where learners write electron arrangements and look for the hidden property behind groups and periods.
slo.safetyNotes: No hazardous materials. Paper cards only. Keep walkways clear when groups move to the wall chart. Learners should handle scissors, if used for cutting cards, with care.

LESSONS.overview: Mwalimu Achieng reminds the class of the Lesson 1 puzzle. Wanjiku, Otieno, Amina and Kipchoge, in a Grade 10 class in Kisumu, had sorted the Element Cards by mass, yet Li (7), Na (23) and K (39) behave alike, and Ne and Ar do not react at all. Learners predict how the first 20 elements should be ordered. They then observe a short historical data set: Mendeleev's 1869 mass-based order with gaps, and Moseley's 1913 finding. They re-arrange the cards by atomic number into 4 rows (periods) and columns (groups), and notice that Ar (A_r 40) must come before K (A_r 39). Learners then explain the meaning of groups and periods, add questions to the DQB, and add the first piece to the Class Model: order is by atomic number, and columns hold elements with similar behaviour (Li, Na, K together; Ne and Ar together). The reason for this similarity is the open question that carries into Lesson 3.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners work in groups of 4 with their Element Cards (H to Ca). Task: 'If you must line up all 20 cards in ONE order so that a chemist anywhere in Nairobi, Mombasa or Kisumu could find any element, which number on the card would you use: atomic number Z or relative atomic mass A_r? Write your prediction and one reason.' Each learner then writes a prediction: 'Where will K (Z19, A_r 39) and Ar (Z18, A_r 40) go if I order by mass? If I order by atomic number?' They also predict how many rows and columns the table will need and which cards will sit in the same column as Li and Na, linking back to the phenomenon of elements that behave alike.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Last lesson we sorted the cards and found a puzzle: Li, Na and K are very different in mass but behave alike. Today we ask: what is the best number to order elements by?' Distribute cards. Give 3 minutes of silent individual writing before group talk. WAIT TIME: after asking 'Which number would you use, Z or A_r, and why?', wait 10-15 seconds before taking answers. Cold-call 4 learners (e.g. Wanjiku, Otieno, Amina and Kipchoge's group representatives) to share predictions. Record the tally of Z versus A_r on the board without judging. Say: 'Hold on to your prediction. The evidence will tell us who is right.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Prediction with reasoning (Predict-Observe-Explain): committing to a written prediction before seeing the evidence activates prior knowledge from Lesson 1 and creates a need to know, so learners compare their ideas with the evidence in the Observe Phase.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that at least 80% of learners wrote a prediction with a reason. Look for use of ideas from Lesson 1 (mass sorting leaves puzzles). Note how many chose Z and how many chose A_r, and whether any predicted a problem for Ar and K. Misconception to listen for: 'heavier atoms must always come later.'

framework.learnerExperience: Part A (10 minutes): Learners study a Historical Data Sheet. Mendeleev (Russian chemist, 1869) ordered the elements by increasing atomic mass and placed those with similar properties in the same column, leaving gaps for elements not yet discovered and predicting their properties. Moseley (English physicist, 1913) showed that the true basis of the order is atomic number (number of protons). Part B (10 minutes): Using a data table of Z, A_r, group and period for H to Ca, learners arrange their Element Cards on a grid: H and He in period 1; Li to Ne in period 2; Na to Ar in period 3; K and Ca in period 4. Groups are placed in columns: group 1 (H, Li, Na, K), group 2 (Be, Mg, Ca), groups 13 to 18 (B to Ne, Al to Ar), with Li, Na, K aligned in a column and Ne and Ar aligned in group 18 with He. They record observations: the order when sorted by A_r versus Z; the pair Ar (Z18, A_r 40) and K (Z19, A_r 39); and Ca (A_r 40), which has the same A_r as Ar but sits in a different group.
framework.teacherMoves: Circulate with the prompts: 'Show me where Li, Na and K landed. What do you notice about their column?' and 'Run your finger along period 3. What changes from Na to Ar?' Point to the Ar and K cards: 'If we order strictly by mass, which comes first? What happens to the pattern?' WAIT TIME: after the Ar/K question, wait 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 3 groups to report where they placed Ar and K and what they saw. Cold-call 2 more learners to name one gap Mendeleev might have left. Stress that a column is a GROUP and a row is a PERIOD. Ask learners to count the rows and columns and note that H and He are in period 1 only. Tell groups that placing a card by atomic number sometimes puts a heavier atom BEFORE a lighter one. Ask: 'What does that tell you about mass as the basis of order?' Do not yet explain why elements in a column behave alike; say: 'Keep that question. Write it on a sticky note for the DQB.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Data-pattern analysis with a physical model: handling the cards on a grid lets learners see patterns in rows and columns directly and notice the anomaly (Ar before K), so the evidence challenges the mass-based prediction.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: cards placed correctly in 4 periods and the correct groups (at least 18 of 20 cards correctly placed); Li, Na and K in one column and Ne and Ar in group 18; learners point out that Ar (40) comes before K (39) and give atomic number as the reason. Check the Observation Sheet for accurate recording of A_r and Z. Look for the misconception that 'period' means column.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners write a claim-evidence-reasoning (CER) paragraph in their notebooks: Claim: what is the correct basis for ordering the elements? Evidence: at least two pieces of data (e.g. Ar Z18 A_r 40 comes before K Z19 A_r 39; Li 7, Na 23 and K 39 line up in one column even though their masses differ greatly; Ca A_r 40 equals Ar A_r 40 but is in a different group). Reasoning: why atomic number gives a consistent order while mass does not, and how Mendeleev's gaps and Moseley's work fit together. They then use their table to answer: (a) What is a group? What is a period? (b) Which period and group is Mg in? (c) Which elements are in the same group as Cl? (d) Predict where an element with Z = 21 would be placed next. Pairs share explanations with another pair.
framework.teacherMoves: Model one sentence frame: 'I claim that elements are ordered by ___ because the data show ___.' Say: 'Use numbers from your table, not just words.' WAIT TIME: after posing 'Why did Mendeleev's mass ordering mostly work and yet fail for Ar and K?', wait 10-15 seconds, then allow pair talk for 2 minutes. Cold-call 4 pairs; ask a fifth learner to restate a peer's idea ('Who can say that in your own words?'). Clarify with the scientific summary: Mendeleev (1869) ordered by mass and left gaps; Moseley (1913) showed atomic number is the true basis; the modern table uses atomic number. Define: group = vertical column (1 to 18), period = horizontal row. Connect to the phenomenon: 'So Li, Na and K, which are very different in mass, share a column. But we have not yet explained WHY elements in a column behave alike. That is our job in Lesson 3.' Do not teach electron arrangement in detail now.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) with peer explanation: structuring an argument from the table data forces learners to connect evidence to the concept of atomic number, and peer restating exposes gaps in reasoning.
framework.formativeAssessment: Collect 6 notebooks. Success criteria: the claim names atomic number; at least two data points cited correctly (Ar/K; Li, Na, K same group or Ca/Ar same A_r); correct definitions of group and period; correct answers to (b) period 3, group 2, and (c) F (and Br beyond the first 20 elements not required). Look for misconceptions such as 'groups are rows' or 'Moseley replaced Mendeleev's idea entirely' (his gaps and column patterns were still useful).

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the DQB started in Lesson 1. In groups, they write on sticky notes (1) one thing they now understand (e.g. 'Order is by atomic number, not mass'), and (2) one new question (e.g. 'Why do Li, Na and K sit in one column and react alike?', 'Why does period 2 have 8 elements?', 'What makes Ne and Ar in the same group do nothing?', 'Why is H in group 1 if it is not like the metals?', 'What did Mendeleev predict in his gaps?'). Each group places two notes on the DQB under 'Answered so far' or 'Still wondering', and they sort the notes into categories such as History, Groups and Periods, and Why Elements Behave Alike.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Our wall should show what we know and what we still need to find out.' Provide each group 2 sticky notes. Cold-call 3 groups to read out and justify a question and say where it belongs. WAIT TIME: after asking 'Which of these questions might the number of electrons help us answer?', wait 10-15 seconds, then take 2 responses. Circle or star questions that link to electron arrangement, the phenomenon, and the Li/Na/K and Ne/Ar patterns. Tell learners: 'Next lesson we write electron arrangements to test these ideas.' Mark questions answered today (e.g. Why is Ar before K?) with a tick and the lesson number.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board (question tracking): publicly sorting questions into answered and open ones makes learning progress visible and keeps the phenomenon at the centre of the unit.
framework.formativeAssessment: Count the number of notes that show a new, productive question connecting columns or rows to the behaviour of elements. Look for learners moving from 'what' questions to 'why' questions. At least one question per group should link to the hidden property that explains the patterns. Note groups that only repeat Lesson 1 questions.

framework.learnerExperience: At the Class Model poster, 'Electron Arrangement Model', learners add the first revision for Lesson 2. In groups they draw a 4-row grid with the first 20 elements arranged by atomic number, label rows 'Periods 1 to 4' and columns 'Groups 1 to 18', and mark the column containing Li, Na and K and the column containing He, Ne and Ar. They add a note in a different colour: 'Order is by atomic number (Moseley, 1913), not mass (Mendeleev, 1869). Ar (40) comes before K (39).' They also add a labelled question mark box: 'What hidden property makes elements in one column behave alike and elements in one row change gradually?' Each learner copies the model into their notebook and writes one sentence predicting what that hidden property might be.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'A model is our best explanation so far. It will change as evidence grows.' Ask a volunteer group (e.g. Kipchoge's group) to draw while others direct: 'Where does K go? Where does Ar go? How do you know?' WAIT TIME: after asking 'What is still missing from our model that would explain why Li, Na and K react alike?', wait 10-15 seconds before cold-calling 3 learners. Accept ideas such as 'something inside the atom' and write them as hypotheses without confirming. Link to the next lesson: 'In Lesson 3 we will write electron arrangements for H to Ca and look for a pattern that matches groups and periods.' Ask learners to complete the exit ticket: 'Why is argon placed before potassium in the periodic table even though argon is heavier?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model building: adding evidence-based elements to a shared Class Model, while marking what is unexplained, lets learners see how new evidence refines their explanation of the phenomenon.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check the model for a correctly labelled grid (periods as rows, groups as columns), Ar before K, and a statement of atomic number as the basis. Exit ticket success criterion: answer states that elements are ordered by atomic number (protons), not mass, with Ar Z18 before K Z19. Record learners whose hypothesis about the hidden property is plausible (for example, something that changes by one from element to element) for follow-up in Lesson 3.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: Which learners still believe that heavier atoms must come later, and which used the Ar/K data to revise that idea? Did every group correctly identify groups as columns and periods as rows? Which DQB questions already point toward electron arrangement, and how will I use them to launch Lesson 3? Did I keep to the lesson boundaries by leaving the explanation of why elements in a column behave alike for later lessons?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: When the first 20 Element Cards were arranged by atomic number into 4 periods (rows) and groups (columns), Li, Na and K fell in one column and He, Ne and Ar in another. Ar (Z18, A_r 40) had to be placed before K (Z19, A_r 39), and Ca (A_r 40) had the same A_r as Ar but sat in a different group.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Mendeleev (1869) ordered elements by atomic mass and left gaps for undiscovered elements. Moseley (1913) showed that atomic number is the true basis of order, and the modern table uses atomic number. A group is a vertical column and a period is a horizontal row.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Mass ordering fails for Ar and K, but atomic number gives a consistent order. The table places elements that behave alike, such as Li, Na and K, in the same group even though their masses differ. The hidden property that causes these patterns is still to be explained and will be explored in Lesson 3.

LESSONS.title: Writing Electron Arrangements: Reading Group and Period from s and p Notation
LESSONS.duration: 40 minutes (one lesson; extend to 80 minutes if double period)
LESSONS.aresKeywords: electron arrangement, energy level, s and p notation, outer electrons, valence electrons, group number, period number, atomic number, Li, Na, K, Ne, Ar

slo.purpose: Learners write the electron arrangements of the first 20 elements in energy-level form (e.g. 2,8,1) and in s and p notation (e.g. 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s1), and use them to read the group number and period number of each element. This gives the 'hidden property' behind the Lesson 2 table of groups and periods that the driving question asks about.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson the learner should be able to: (a) relate the position of an element in the periodic table to its electron arrangement. Learners know that Z = number of electrons in a neutral atom; that energy levels fill in the order 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s; that s holds up to 2 electrons and p up to 6; that period number = number of occupied energy levels; that group 1 and 2 = number of outer electrons, and groups 13 to 18 = outer electrons + 10 (He, with 2 outer electrons, is in group 18).
slo.skills: Writing electron arrangements in two forms; counting outer (valence) electrons; reading group and period from notation; identifying patterns in data (NGSS: Analyzing and Interpreting Data); using a pattern as evidence to construct an explanation (NGSS: Constructing Explanations); Communication and Collaboration: listening keenly and using open questions while discussing with peers.
slo.attitudes: Appreciate the role of electron arrangement in the development of the periodic table. Show tolerance (Peace) when peers disagree about where an electron goes, and appreciate the contribution of scientists such as Mendeleev and Moseley (Citizenship). Practise analytical thinking (Life skills) when predicting an element's position from its notation.
slo.keyInquiry: How does electron arrangement influence the arrangement of elements in the periodic table? (Lesson focus: What do the electron arrangements of Li, Na and K have in common, and how can we read group and period from them?)
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 2 arranged H to Ca by atomic number into groups (columns) and periods (rows) but did not say why an element belongs in a particular column. Lesson 3 supplies the evidence: electron arrangements for H to Ca. Learners discover that group tracks outer electrons and period tracks occupied energy levels, so Li, Na and K (masses 7, 23, 39) share a column because each has 1 outer electron. This sets up Lesson 4 (families and reactivity patterns) and Lesson 5 (stability).
slo.safetyNotes: No hazardous chemicals are used. Use paper, counters (bottle tops or beans) and the Element Cards. Keep the floor clear of dropped counters. Learners work in groups of 4 and must not eat the beans or maize grains used as counters.

LESSONS.overview: Mwalimu Achieng reminds the class of the Lesson 2 table: H to Ca arranged by atomic number into groups and periods. Then she asks the puzzle again: why do Li (7), Na (23) and K (39) sit in the same column and all react vigorously with water, while neighbours Na and Mg, or Cl and Ar, behave very differently? Learners first predict what might be the same inside Li, Na and K atoms. In the Observe phase they use counters (beans and maize grains) to build electron arrangements for the first 20 elements, write them in energy-level form (2,8,1) and s and p notation (1s2 2s2 2p6 3s1), and fill a data table. In the Explain phase they look for patterns linking outer electrons to group and occupied levels to period, and test the rules on Ne, Ar, K and Ca. The DQB is updated with new questions (why do outer electrons matter for reactions? why is a full outer level special?) and the Class Model 'Electron Arrangement Model' is revised to show the first version of the rule: group from outer electrons, period from occupied energy levels.

framework.learnerExperience: (5 min) Learners recall the Lesson 2 table of groups and periods for H to Ca displayed on the board. Mwalimu Achieng shows the Element Cards for Li (Z3, A_r 7), Na (Z11, A_r 23) and K (Z19, A_r 39), which sit in the same column, and the cards for Na, Mg, Ne and Ar. Individually, learners silently write a prediction in their notebooks: 'The atoms of Li, Na and K must have this in common inside them: ___. Na and Mg differ in this way: ___.' They then draw a quick sketch of where they think the electrons of a sodium atom (11 electrons) are placed. They share with a partner (think-pair-share) and a few ideas go on the board. This links directly to the phenomenon: elements with very different masses fall in the same column and react alike.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Look at the Lesson 2 table. Li, Na and K are in the same column but their masses are 7, 23 and 39. Something hidden must be the same inside these atoms. Write your prediction silently.' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after asking: 'What could be the same inside Li, Na and K atoms?' before taking any answer. Then say 'Turn to your partner and compare for one minute.' Cold-call 3 pairs (for example Wanjiku and Otieno's group, Amina's group, Kipchoge's group, as names in examples only; use your own learners' names) with: 'Tell us your partner's idea, not your own.' Record all ideas on the board WITHOUT judging them as right or wrong. Ask: 'What would you need to see to check this idea?' Circulate and note learners who mention electrons, energy levels or shells.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Think-Pair-Share with prediction recording. Writing a prediction before instruction makes learners' prior ideas visible and gives them a stake in the evidence; hearing a partner's idea first lowers the risk of speaking and builds the habit of listening keenly. Learners revisit these predictions in the Explain phase to confirm, revise or reject them using evidence.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) at least 80% of learners have a written prediction and a sketch before the pair talk; (2) count how many predictions mention electrons or energy levels (note names for follow-up); (3) note misconceptions, e.g. 'same number of neutrons', 'same mass', 'same colour'. Record these on the teacher checklist to return to in the Explain phase.

framework.learnerExperience: (15 min) In groups of 4, learners use counters (beans for electrons, with a paper 'energy level' diagram of circles for levels 1 to 4) to build the electron arrangement of atoms of H to Ca. Rules on the worksheet: level 1 holds up to 2 electrons (1s); level 2 holds up to 8 (2s then 2p); level 3 filled to 8 in this lesson (3s then 3p); then 4s takes the next electrons for K and Ca. Each learner is given 5 or 6 elements, so the group covers all 20. For each element they record: (i) Z, (ii) energy-level form e.g. Na 2,8,1; (iii) s and p notation, e.g. Na 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s1; (iv) number of outer electrons; (v) number of occupied energy levels. They copy the Lesson 2 group and period from the table next to their results. They complete a class data table: H 1s1; He 1s2; Li 1s2 2s1; Be 1s2 2s2; B 1s2 2s2 2p1; C 2p2; N 2p3; O 2p4; F 2p5; Ne 2p6; Na 3s1; Mg 3s2; Al 3s2 3p1; Si 3p2; P 3p3; S 3p4; Cl 3p5; Ar 3p6; K 4s1; Ca 4s2. Groups compare results with a neighbouring group to check agreement.
framework.teacherMoves: Model one example on the board with the whole class: sodium, Z11. Say: 'Sodium has 11 electrons. Watch how I fill 1s with 2, then 2s with 2, then 2p with 6. That is 10. One electron remains, so it goes into 3s.' Write 2,8,1 and 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s1 side by side and explain that the numbers in front of s and p are the energy levels and the small superscripts count electrons. Then release the groups. Circulate and ask: 'Which electrons are in the outermost energy level?' and 'How many energy levels have electrons in them?' Prompt struggling groups: 'How many electrons does the 2p sub-level hold when full?' Use WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after each question before giving a hint. Cold-call 2 learners per group to read out their group's results for Li, Na and K. Say: 'Place your finger on the outer electrons of Li, Na and K. What do you notice?' Stop at 12 minutes and ask each group to check the Ne, Ar, K and Ca rows carefully, because they are the ones used later in the Explain phase. Note the common errors: putting K's last electron in 3d or 3p, or writing 2p before 2s.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Modelling with physical representations (counters on level diagrams), moving from concrete to symbolic. Learners physically place electrons level by level, then translate to the 2,8,1 and s and p forms side by side, which shows that both notations describe the same arrangement. Building every element from the same filling rules turns individual results into a data set that can be searched for patterns (NGSS: Developing and Using Models; Analyzing and Interpreting Data).
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: learners correctly build Na as 2,8,1 and 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s1 without help; the total of the superscripts equals Z for each element (self-check); the counters on the paper diagram match the written notation; groups agree in the neighbour-group check. Spot-check Cl (2,8,7; 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p5) and K (2,8,8,1; ...3p6 4s1). Use a 3-finger self-rating (3 = confident, 2 = need hints, 1 = lost) at the end of the phase and note the learners showing 1.

framework.learnerExperience: (10 min) Using the completed data table, groups look for patterns. Task 1: highlight the outer electron count for Li, Na and K, and for Be, Mg and Ca, and compare it with the group number from the Lesson 2 table. They find group 1 elements have 1 outer electron and group 2 elements have 2. Task 2: look at B to Ne and Al to Ar. Outer electrons are 3 to 8 and groups are 13 to 18, so group = outer electrons + 10 (He has 2 outer electrons but is in group 18, with a full 1s2). Task 3: count occupied energy levels for H and He (1), Li to Ne (2), Na to Ar (3), K and Ca (4), and compare with the period number. Task 4: test the rules with a 'mystery atom': 2,8,6 (1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p4), which gives group 16, period 3 and identifies it as sulfur (S). They then write an explanation: 'Li, Na and K are in the same group because ___; Na is in period 3 because ___.' They revisit their Predict-phase ideas and say which were supported by evidence. Finally they discuss: 'Ne (2,8) and Ar (2,8,8) both have a full outer level and do not react at all. What might that mean?' (the stability idea is developed in Lesson 5, so they only record the pattern for now).
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Look only at the data table. What pattern do you see between outer electrons and group number?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 3 learners for Task 1 and 3 for Task 3, using the question: 'What is your evidence from the table?' Press for evidence: 'Which rows of the table support what you just said?' When learners say 'group number equals outer electrons', ask: 'Does that work for chlorine, which has 7 outer electrons and is in group 17?' to prompt them to refine the rule for groups 13 to 18. Point out the K and Ar mass puzzle from Lesson 2: 'Atomic number still decides the order, and now we see why: each step in Z adds one electron, so the arrangement changes step by step.' Use the mystery atom as a quick whiteboard check: all learners show their answer at once, then cold-call 2 to explain their reasoning. Link back to the phenomenon: 'Li, Na and K have different masses but the same outer electron count. Does this help to explain why they sit in the same column?' Avoid saying why they react the same; say: 'We will test in the next lesson whether outer electrons also explain how they react.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Pattern-seeking with claim-evidence-reasoning (CER). Learners state a claim (e.g. 'group number is linked to outer electrons'), cite specific rows from the data table as evidence, and give reasoning for why the pattern holds across several elements. Applying the rule to a mystery atom tests whether the pattern is general. This builds the cause-and-effect link between electron arrangement and position in the periodic table (NGSS: Constructing Explanations; Patterns).
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: learners cite specific data (for example 'Na is 2,8,1 with 1 outer electron and it is in group 1') rather than asserting the rule; they correctly identify the mystery atom as sulfur in group 16, period 3; they explain why He is placed in group 18 despite having 2 outer electrons; they correctly state that K is in period 4 because it has electrons in 4 energy levels. Collect a written exit sentence from each learner: 'Li, Na and K are in the same group because ___.' Look for 'same number of outer electrons' as the key idea. Misconception to watch for: confusing the number of electrons in total with the number in the outer level.

framework.learnerExperience: (5 min) Learners return to the Driving Question Board (the class wall chart started in Lesson 1). Individually they write one new question on a sticky note based on today's evidence, for example 'Why do atoms with 1 outer electron react with water?', 'Why are atoms with a full outer level, like Ne and Ar, unreactive?', 'Why does Mg (2 outer electrons) behave differently from Na (1 outer electron)?', 'Do all elements follow the group = outer electrons rule? What about iron and copper?' Then they place their notes under suitable headings (Pattern in the table, Reactivity, Ions and compounds). They also tick questions already answered, such as 'What is the same inside Li, Na and K atoms?'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'What new question has today's data made you ask? Write it so that someone from another group can understand it.' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before learners start writing. Select 3 notes at random and cold-call the authors to read them aloud; ask the class: 'Which lesson do you think might help us answer this?' Group similar questions together, and point out that questions about reactivity and full outer levels will be addressed in Lessons 4 and 5, and questions about ions and formulae later in the sequence. Mark the question 'What is the same inside Li, Na and K atoms?' as 'partly answered: same outer electron count'. Do not answer the new questions yet.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Question generation and sorting on a Driving Question Board. Writing questions from evidence keeps learners' own curiosity driving the unit and shows how today's pattern leads to the next investigation. Sorting questions into categories helps learners see the storyline of the whole unit.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: each learner posts at least one question; at least half of the questions refer to outer electrons, full outer levels, or reactions (showing that learners link electron arrangement to behaviour); questions use today's vocabulary (energy level, outer electrons, group, period). Note learners whose questions are only about copying notation, and follow up with them individually.

framework.learnerExperience: (5 min) Learners gather around the Class Model poster 'Electron Arrangement Model'. As a class they add a new section: 'Inside the atom: electrons are arranged in energy levels (1s; 2s 2p; 3s 3p; 4s).' They add two rules to the poster: 'Group number (groups 1, 2) = number of outer electrons; groups 13 to 18 = outer electrons + 10' and 'Period number = number of occupied energy levels'. They draw Li, Na and K as three level diagrams (2,1; 2,8,1; 2,8,8,1 for K) with the outer electron coloured in, and add a note: 'Same outer electrons, same group, different mass'. Each group also adds a labelled sketch of an atom of their choice (for example Cl, 2,8,7, in group 17, period 3 for the water treatment in Nairobi and Mombasa). They add a 'What we still need to explain' box: why outer electrons affect how an element reacts, and why the full outer levels of Ne and Ar matter.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Our model must explain the pattern we found. What belongs on the poster, and what evidence supports it?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 4 learners, one for each item to be added, asking 'What is your evidence?' before adding anything to the poster. Ask: 'Which part of the phenomenon can our model already explain, and which part can it not yet explain?' Guide learners to see that it explains the column pattern (Li, Na, K) and the row pattern (period), but not yet the reactivity of Li, Na and K or the lack of reaction of Ne and Ar. Write these gaps in the 'still need to explain' box. Briefly connect to the history: Moseley used atomic number to order elements; today we see that atomic number sets the number of electrons and hence the arrangement. Close with the exit slip: 'Write the s and p notation for chlorine and state its group and period.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision (NGSS: Developing and Using Models). Learners add new evidence-based components to a shared model and explicitly list what the model cannot yet explain, which sets the purpose for Lessons 4 and 5. A visible, revisable model helps learners see how each lesson builds on the previous one toward explaining the driving question.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: the exit slip shows Cl as 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p5, group 17, period 3 (or 2,8,7); learners can point to the poster and explain why Li, Na and K are in the same group; the poster includes the group and period rules and level diagrams; learners identify at least one thing the model cannot yet explain. Collect exit slips and sort them into three piles (correct, minor error, needs reteach) for planning the start of Lesson 4.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect: (1) Did learners generate the group and period rules from the data table, or did they only copy the rule from you? Which questions prompted real reasoning? (2) Which notation errors were most common (for example putting K's last electron in 3p or 3d, writing 2p before 2s, or forgetting that total superscripts must equal Z)? Plan a quick correction for the start of Lesson 4. (3) Did learners confuse 'group = outer electrons' with groups 13 to 18 (outer electrons + 10), and did He cause confusion? (4) Which learners hesitated to speak in the Think-Pair-Share, and how can you give them a role next time? (5) Were the Kenyan contexts (Kisumu classroom, chlorine in Nairobi and Mombasa, potassium in Kericho farms) used to keep the phenomenon in view? (6) What do the exit slips and DQB questions tell you about readiness for Lesson 4 on families and reactivity? Note any learners who need extra support with counting electrons.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We built the electron arrangements of H to Ca using counters and wrote them in energy-level form (e.g. Na 2,8,1) and s and p notation (e.g. Na 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s1). We noticed that Li (2,1), Na (2,8,1) and K (2,8,8,1) each have 1 outer electron, and that Ne (2,8) and Ar (2,8,8) have full outer levels.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Group number is decided by the number of outer electrons (group 1 and 2 = number of outer electrons; groups 13 to 18 = outer electrons + 10, with He, 1s2, in group 18). Period number equals the number of occupied energy levels. Elements in the same group have the same outer electron count even though their masses differ.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Li, Na and K sit in the same column despite masses of 7, 23 and 39 because each atom has 1 outer electron, while neighbours such as Na and Mg differ because their outer electron counts differ (1 and 2). Electron arrangement, the hidden property that follows from atomic number, therefore decides where an element is placed in the periodic table. We still need to explain why outer electrons control how elements react.
