LESSONS.title: Chemical Families and Reactivity Patterns: Why Li, Na and K Behave Alike
LESSONS.duration: 40 minutes (one lesson; Predict 5 min, Observe 12 min, Explain 10 min, DQB 5 min, Model 8 min)
LESSONS.aresKeywords: chemical families, alkali metals, alkaline earth metals, halogens, noble gases, transition elements, outer electrons, reactivity trend, group 1, group 17, group 18

slo.purpose: Learners name the five chemical families, locate them by group, and use outer electron count to explain why elements in a family react alike and why reactivity changes down a group, taking us closer to answering how electron arrangement influences the arrangement of elements in the periodic table.
slo.knowledge: Alkali metals (group 1) have 1 outer electron; alkaline earth metals (group 2) have 2; halogens (group 17) have 7; noble gases (group 18) have a full outer level (8; He has 2); transition elements lie between group 2 and group 13 from period 4 onward and include Fe and Cu. Reactivity of alkali metals with water increases down the group: Li < Na < K. Mg and Ca are in group 2, with Ca more reactive than Mg. Ne and Ar do not react. Cl2 (and fluoride compounds) are used in water treatment in Nairobi and Mombasa.
slo.skills: Observing and recording a reaction (demonstration or simulation); analysing and interpreting data (NGSS SEP: Analyzing and Interpreting Data); identifying patterns (Crosscutting: Patterns); constructing explanations using evidence (SEP: Constructing Explanations); communicating and collaborating in groups using open questions.
slo.attitudes: Learners appreciate the role of electron arrangement in the development of the periodic table; show tolerance and compassion when peers' predictions differ (Peace); work with peers respectfully on shared evidence (Citizenship, social cohesion); apply analytical thinking (Life skills) to patterns in data.
slo.keyInquiry: How does electron arrangement influence the arrangement of elements in the periodic table? (Sub-strand guiding question from the teacher's phenomenon; the KICD question 'How do chemical bonds influence the properties of substances?' belongs to 1.4 Chemical Bonding and is the forward link.)
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 3 gave learners the rule that group number comes from outer electrons and period from occupied energy levels. Lesson 1 left the puzzle that Li, Na and K are alike despite different masses. Lesson 4 names the families, gathers reaction evidence, and links family behaviour to outer electron count. It sets up Lesson 5 (why atoms lose or gain electrons to reach a full outer level), which explains the noble gases' inertness.
slo.safetyNotes: Preferably use a teacher-led video or simulation of Na and K with water. If a live demonstration is done: only the teacher handles the metals with forceps; use a rice-grain-sized piece of Na (and never K live); use a large trough half-filled with water behind a clear screen; learners stand at least 2 metres back and wear safety goggles; keep metals stored under oil, dry cut pieces on filter paper, and dispose of leftovers as the teacher directs. Li may be shown in a very small piece. Do not let learners touch alkali metals. Chlorine gas is NOT demonstrated; use photographs and a reading about water treatment. Wash hands after handling any materials. Have a bucket of sand and a fire blanket ready, and never use water on a metal fire.

LESSONS.overview: Mwalimu Achieng opens by asking learners to revisit the Element Cards and the Lesson 1 puzzle: Li (A_r 7), Na (23) and K (39) are very different in mass yet all react vigorously with water, while Ne and Ar do not react at all. Learners predict the order of reactivity and what feature of the atoms makes them alike. They then gather evidence from a teacher demonstration or simulation of Li, Na and K with water, and from data cards on Mg and Ca, Ne and Ar, Cl and F (water treatment in Nairobi, Mombasa and Lake Victoria supplies), and Fe and Cu (transition elements). Groups of four (Wanjiku, Otieno, Amina and Kipchoge are example names) build a Family Table linking each family to group number and outer electrons from Lesson 3. In the Explain phase they construct a claim-evidence-reasoning statement that family behaviour follows outer electron count. New questions are added to the Driving Question Board (DQB), and the Class Model (Electron Arrangement Model) is revised to add families and the idea that outer electrons decide behaviour. Why atoms lose or gain electrons is deliberately left to Lesson 5.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners look at the Element Cards for Li, Na, K, Ne and Ar (symbol, Z, A_r and properties, but no positions). Individually, in 2 minutes, they write on a sticky note or in their notebooks: (1) the order in which Li, Na and K will react with water from slowest to fastest, and (2) one reason why Li, Na and K, with masses 7, 23 and 39, might behave alike. They use Lesson 3 to write the outer electron count of each (Li 2,1; Na 2,8,1; K 2,8,8,1) and predict what Ne (2,8) and Ar (2,8,8) will do. They pair-share and draw a quick sketch of what they expect to see when a piece of sodium meets water.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the five cards on the board. Say: "In Lesson 1 we saw that Li, Na and K behave alike even though their masses are very different. Today we find out what family they belong to and whether we can predict who reacts fastest. Write your prediction first, quietly." Give 2 minutes of silent writing, then WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after asking: "What do Li, Na and K have in common according to the electron arrangements you wrote in Lesson 3?" Then cold-call 4 learners (e.g. Wanjiku, Otieno, Amina, Kipchoge) for predictions without judging them, saying: "Thank you, I am recording that on the board. We will test it with evidence." Tally the predicted orders on the board. Accept all predictions and do not reveal the answer. Remind the class to respect different views (Peace).
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (prediction stage) with a Think-Pair-Share: committing to a prediction in writing exposes prior ideas, such as 'heavier metals react faster', so that later evidence can confirm or challenge them. It links to the phenomenon by asking what hidden property makes elements of different masses alike.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check: (a) at least 80% of learners wrote a predicted order and a reason; (b) learners correctly state outer electron counts for Li, Na and K as 1 from their Lesson 3 arrangements; (c) listen for misconceptions such as 'mass decides reactivity' or 'neon is just a slow reactor'; note names and tally the types of prediction on the board for use in the Explain phase.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners gather evidence in three stations of 4 minutes each (or as a whole-class sequence if resources are limited). Station/Part A: watch the teacher demonstration or video/simulation of Li, Na and K in water. They record in a table: does it float or sink, melt, fizz (rate), flame colour, and relative speed. Expected qualitative observations: Li fizzes steadily and floats; Na melts into a ball, darts and fizzes fast; K melts, burns with a lilac flame and is very vigorous. They test a drop of universal indicator or red litmus in the water after to note it turns alkaline (the products are LiOH, NaOH, KOH solutions, with the equation left for Lesson 9). Part B: Data cards. Card 1: Mg and Ca with water or dilute acid: Ca reacts faster than Mg; both are group 2 with 2 outer electrons (Mg 2,8,2; Ca 2,8,8,2). Card 2: Ne and Ar: no reactions; they have full outer levels (2,8 and 2,8,8). Card 3: Cl2 and fluoride compounds in water treatment in Nairobi and Mombasa and in water drawn from Lake Victoria in Kisumu: halogens have 7 outer electrons (F 2,7; Cl 2,8,7) and are reactive non-metals. Card 4: Fe and Cu, transition elements from period 4 (Fe rusts in Kisumu's humid air and in mabati roofs; Cu is used in electrical wires), which form more than one ion (Fe2+ and Fe3+, Cu+ and Cu2+), a pattern not predicted by outer electron count alone, to be explored in Lesson 7. Learners complete a Family Table with the columns: family, group, example elements, outer electrons, behaviour observed.
framework.teacherMoves: Set safety rules first: "Everyone stays behind the line, goggles on, no touching the metals." If demonstrating, cut each piece at the front and say aloud: "Watch the metal's surface, the speed, and any flame. Record exactly what you see, not what you expected." Run the sequence Li, then Na (and show K by video only). Pause after each: "What did you observe? Describe it without explaining it yet." WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before taking answers. Cold-call 3 learners per metal to give one observation each. For Part B, circulate and ask groups: "Which of these elements react and which do not? What do the reactive ones in the same column share?" and "How many outer electrons does each have?" Prompt for the families by name: "We call group 1 the alkali metals, group 2 the alkaline earth metals, group 17 the halogens, group 18 the noble gases, and the block between group 2 and 13 from period 4 the transition elements." Collect the observations on a class chart, ordering Li < Na < K for reactivity. Point out that Ar (A_r 40) and Ca (A_r 40) have the same mass but opposite behaviour (Ar does not react, Ca does), reinforcing the Lesson 1 puzzle.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Data table and pattern-finding (Analyzing and Interpreting Data; Patterns): recording observations in a Family Table, separate from explanations, lets learners see that reactivity increases down group 1 and that behaviour tracks the column, not the mass. Using a demonstration/simulation and data cards provides multiple sources of evidence.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: learners' tables record float/melt/fizz/flame for Li, Na, K accurately and in the order Li < Na < K; they label at least four families correctly with group numbers; they write 1, 2, 7 and full for outer electrons in the correct rows; they state that Ne and Ar showed no reaction. Walk around with a checklist; ask any group with a wrong family-to-group match: "Check your Lesson 3 arrangement again. How many outer electrons does it have?"

framework.learnerExperience: In groups of four, learners use the Family Table to write a claim-evidence-reasoning (CER) statement: Claim: elements in the same family behave alike because they have the same number of outer electrons. Evidence: Li (2,1), Na (2,8,1) and K (2,8,8,1) all have 1 outer electron and all react with water, though their masses are 7, 23 and 39; Ne (2,8) and Ar (2,8,8) have full outer levels and do not react. Reasoning: outer electrons decide how an atom behaves, so the group number tells us the family. They then answer: (1) Why are Na and Mg, neighbours in period 3, so different? (Na has 1 outer electron, Mg has 2.) (2) Why do Na and Ne, with similar masses 23 and 20, behave so differently? (3) Predict: rubidium (Rb) is below K in group 1; will it be more or less reactive than K, and why? (More reactive; same outer electron count, trend continues down.) (4) Chlorine is in group 17: how many outer electrons, and why is it classed with fluorine? Learners state that they do not yet know why the number of outer electrons causes such behaviour, and write this as a question for the DQB (this is left for Lesson 5). They compare their Lesson 4 predictions with the evidence and revise them.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Use only your evidence to complete the claim. Every reason must point to outer electrons." Circulate and ask: "Which observation supports your claim?" and "Does mass explain it? Look at Ar 40 and Ca 40." Use talk moves: "Who can add to what Amina said?" and "Do you agree or disagree with Otieno, and why?" Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after each question. Cold-call 5 learners from different groups to share one part of their CER, and ask the class to give a thumbs up or down on whether the evidence supports it. Address the misconception that heavier means more reactive across all groups: "Within a group, reactivity increases down the group; across a period, neighbours differ because their outer electron counts differ." Do NOT explain why atoms lose or gain electrons or the stability of full outer levels; say: "That is a great question and Lesson 5 will answer it. Put it on the DQB." Note that for transition elements, Fe and Cu have variable ions that outer electron count alone does not predict; this is explored in Lesson 7.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning with Talk Moves (Constructing Explanations and Engaging in Argument from Evidence): learners must link a general claim to specific data (Li, Na, K; Ne, Ar; Mg, Ca) and to the concept of outer electrons, building a causal chain from the arrangement of electrons to the behaviour of a family. Predicting Rb's reactivity tests whether the pattern transfers to an unseen element, a step toward the Lesson 10 strontium task.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: CER statements that cite at least two pieces of data and mention outer electrons in the reasoning; correct answer that Na and Mg differ because of 1 versus 2 outer electrons; correct prediction that Rb is more reactive than K; no claims that mass causes the similarity. Use a quick exit check: "Complete: Elements in group 1 react alike because ______." Learners who say 'they have similar mass' are grouped for a short re-teach using the Element Cards while others extend with Fr or Cs.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners add new questions and partial answers to the class DQB wall chart started in Lesson 1. They place sticky notes under categories such as 'Answered today', 'New questions' and 'Still puzzling'. Example answered items: 'Why do Li, Na and K behave alike?' (same outer electron count, 1). Example new questions: 'Why do atoms with full outer levels not react?', 'Why does the reactivity of group 1 metals increase down the group?', 'Why do halogens react in the opposite way to alkali metals?', 'Why do iron and copper form more than one kind of ion?', 'Why is chlorine used in water treatment in Nairobi and Mombasa?' Each learner writes at least one question, and pairs decide which lesson might answer it.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Look at the board. What have we answered about our driving question today? What are we still wondering?" Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, then invite 4 learners to read a sticky note aloud and place it. Ask: "Which question connects to what we saw in the sodium reaction?" Move 'Why do Li, Na and K behave alike?' to a 'Partly answered' column and label it 'same outer electrons, Lesson 4'. Tell the class that the 'why full outer levels are stable' question will be tackled in Lesson 5, and the 'Fe and Cu' question in Lesson 7. Praise good questions with a comment such as: "That question will help us explain the phenomenon."
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board as a public record of growing understanding: connecting learner questions to evidence and to future lessons builds ownership and shows that science progresses by turning observations into new questions.
framework.formativeAssessment: Count questions: every learner contributed at least one note; at least half of the notes refer to why or how (causal) rather than what; check that learners correctly sort notes into 'answered' versus 'new'. Note any learner whose question reveals a misconception, such as 'noble gases are unreactive because they are light', and revisit it in Lesson 5.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revise the class poster, 'Electron Arrangement Model'. In groups, they add to the model: (1) the five family names with group numbers (alkali metals group 1, alkaline earth metals group 2, transition elements between group 2 and 13 from period 4, halogens group 17, noble gases group 18); (2) outer electron counts of 1, 2, 7 and full for the four main families; (3) an arrow showing reactivity of alkali metals increasing down group 1 (Li < Na < K); (4) the statement 'Same outer electrons = same family behaviour, regardless of mass'. They also add the label 'Mass does not decide behaviour: Li 7, Na 23, K 39 alike; Na 23 and Ne 20 differ'. Each group draws a mini-diagram of the electron arrangement of one family member, e.g. 2,8,1 for Na and 2,8,7 for Cl, and notes with a question mark the part not yet explained (why outer electrons matter). Individually, learners complete the three-column summary table in their notebooks: What we observed, What we learned, How we can explain it.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Take the model from Lesson 3. What must we add today, based on evidence?" Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 3 groups to propose one addition each and ask the class: "Is there evidence on our chart to support that?" Insist that every addition cite an observation. Mark unexplained parts of the model with a question mark. Ask: "Where in our model does the Rb prediction fit?" Close with: "We now know that the outer electrons give elements a family identity. Next lesson we ask why outer electrons make an atom react or not react." Collect the summary tables as an exit ticket.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Model Revision (Developing and Using Models): updating the Class Model with only evidence-based additions, and marking gaps, shows how a model is improved over time and connects the family patterns to the underlying cause, electron arrangement.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that the revised model includes the correct family-group-outer-electron links and a reactivity trend arrow; check at least 80% of the learners' tables state that outer electrons, not mass, explain family similarity; note any learner who cannot link Ne and Ar to a full outer level. Use the answers as an exit ticket to plan the opening of Lesson 5.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect: Did learners rely on the evidence (Li, Na, K reactions; Ne and Ar; Mg and Ca) rather than on mass to explain the family patterns? Which learners still said 'heavier reacts faster'? Was the safety plan followed, and was the demonstration or simulation visible to everyone in the class? Did I resist explaining why full outer levels are stable, leaving it for Lesson 5? Which DQB questions should open Lesson 5? How well did Kisumu-based contexts such as Lake Victoria water treatment, mabati roofs and Kericho fertilizers help learners connect with the content? What would I change next time about wait time, cold-calling and group roles?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Li fizzes steadily and floats; Na melts into a ball, darts and fizzes fast; K melts, burns with a lilac flame and is very vigorous. Ca reacts faster than Mg. Ne and Ar do not react. Cl and F compounds are used in water treatment in Nairobi and Mombasa. Fe and Cu form more than one ion.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Elements fall into families: alkali metals (group 1, 1 outer electron), alkaline earth metals (group 2, 2 outer electrons), halogens (group 17, 7 outer electrons), noble gases (group 18, full outer level) and transition elements (between group 2 and 13 from period 4). Reactivity of alkali metals increases down the group: Li < Na < K.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Elements in the same family behave alike because they have the same number of outer electrons, not the same mass (Li 7, Na 23 and K 39 all have 1 outer electron). Neighbours such as Na and Mg or Na and Ne differ because their outer electron counts differ. Why a full outer level makes Ne and Ar unreactive is still to be explained in Lesson 5.

LESSONS.title: Stability of Atoms: Why Atoms Lose or Gain Electrons
LESSONS.aresKeywords: stability, full outer energy level, octet, duplet, noble gas arrangement, outer electrons, valence electrons, lose electrons, gain electrons

slo.purpose: Learners use outer electron counts of He, Ne, Ar, Na, Mg, O and Cl to explain why noble gases are unreactive and why other atoms lose or gain electrons to reach a full outer level.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson, the learner should be able to: (1) state that noble gases (He 1s2; Ne 2,8; Ar 2,8,8) have full outer energy levels (duplet for He, octet for Ne and Ar) that are stable; (2) explain that atoms with few outer electrons (Na 1, Mg 2) tend to lose electrons, and atoms with nearly full outer levels (O 6, Cl 7) tend to gain electrons, to reach the noble gas arrangement; (3) relate stability to the phenomenon of why group 1 metals react vigorously while Ne and Ar do not. Linked KICD outcome: relate the position of an element in the periodic table to its electron arrangement (a); and discuss with peers the stability of atoms (loss or gain of electrons).
slo.skills: Developing and using models (NGSS SEP 2): sketch energy-level diagrams and use them to predict whether an atom will lose or gain electrons. Constructing explanations (SEP 6): use evidence of outer electron counts and reactivity to explain stability. Engaging in argument from evidence (SEP 7): defend a claim about the easiest route to a full outer level. Communication and Collaboration: listen keenly and use open questions in group discussion.
slo.attitudes: Appreciate the role of electron arrangement in explaining patterns in the periodic table. Show tolerance and compassion (Peace) by listening to and respectfully challenging peers' predictions. Show social cohesion (PCI) by sharing roles and ideas fairly in groups.
slo.keyInquiry: Why do some atoms, such as Na and Cl, readily lose or gain electrons, while Ne and Ar do not react at all?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lessons 3 and 4 showed that outer electron count decides the group and that noble gases (Ne, Ar) are unreactive while Li, Na, K react vigorously. Lesson 5 supplies the missing reason: a full outer level is stable, so atoms with other outer electron counts change to reach it. This sets up Lesson 6, where learners predict the ions formed and draw dot-and-cross diagrams. It advances the driving question by linking electron arrangement to the ions and compounds elements form.
slo.safetyNotes: This lesson is paper and discussion based with no chemicals. Where the teacher demonstrates or recalls the sodium or potassium water reaction, use only a video or the earlier observations; do not handle alkali metals in class. Keep walkways clear during gallery walk movement. Use blunt-tipped counters and avoid throwing them.

LESSONS.overview: Mwalimu Achieng reminds the class from Lessons 3 and 4 that Ne and Ar do not react while Na, which has one outer electron, reacts vigorously. Learners at their Kisumu school first predict which atoms will gain, lose or keep electrons. They then gather evidence with an electron-counter card sort: using bean and maize seed counters as electrons, they build He, Ne, Ar, Na, Mg, O and Cl, and count how many electrons must move to make a full outer level. In the Explain phase, learners use the 'Claim-Evidence-Reasoning' strategy to explain why Na loses 1 electron, not gains 7, and why Cl gains 1, not loses 7. They then add new questions to the Driving Question Board (DQB) and revise the Class Model ('Electron Arrangement Model') with the stability idea. This answers part of the phenomenon: why elements in different groups behave very differently, and why neighbours like Na, Mg, Ne and Ar differ.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners recall the phenomenon: Li, Na and K react vigorously with water while Ne and Ar do not react at all, and chlorine is used in water treatment in Nairobi and Mombasa. Each learner receives a prediction slip with Ne 2,8; Na 2,8,1; Mg 2,8,2; O 2,6; Cl 2,8,7. On the slip they answer individually: 'Which of these atoms do you think is most stable (least likely to react)? Which will lose electrons, which will gain, and why?' They draw a quick energy-level sketch for one atom and write one sentence of reasoning. Then they pair up with Wanjiku-, Otieno-, Amina- or Kipchoge-style partners to compare and record agreements and disagreements.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the Element Cards for Ne, Na, Cl and the DQB. Say: 'Yesterday we saw that neon and argon sit in group 18 and do not react. Today we ask why. Before I teach anything, I want your honest prediction.' Give 3 minutes of silent writing. Ask: 'Look at Na 2,8,1 and Cl 2,8,7. Which one is closer to Ne 2,8 and which is closer to Ar 2,8,8?' WAIT TIME: 10-15 seconds, no hands up. Cold-call 3 learners: 'Amina, what did you predict for sodium? Why?' Record 2-3 different predictions on the board without judging. Say: 'There are no wrong predictions right now; we will test them with evidence.' Circulate and note who thinks atoms 'want' electrons, to revisit in the Explain phase.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (prior-ideas elicitation) with Think-Pair-Share: writing a prediction before any instruction commits learners to an idea, so that evidence later either supports or challenges it. It makes their thinking visible and gives the class a shared reference to return to.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) learners who link Ne and Ar's lack of reactivity to full outer energy levels or 8 outer electrons; (2) learners who sketch the correct outer electron count for Na (1), Mg (2), O (6) and Cl (7); (3) learners who give a reason beyond 'because it wants to' (such as 'closer to 8'). Tally on a checklist how many correctly sketch two or more atoms. Note misconceptions (e.g. 'atoms need to be full of electrons in total') for the Explain phase.

framework.learnerExperience: In groups of four, learners use an Electron Counter Card Sort. Each group receives a mat with energy-level rings and 30 counters (maize seeds as electrons). Step 1: They build He (1s2, duplet), Ne (2,8) and Ar (2,8,8) and record 'outer electrons: 2, 8, 8' and 'reactivity: none'. Step 2: They build Na (2,8,1), Mg (2,8,2), O (2,6) and Cl (2,8,7). For each, they count (a) how many electrons must be removed to leave a full outer level beneath, and (b) how many must be added to fill the outer level. They complete a table: Atom | Outer electrons | Electrons to lose | Electrons to gain | Easier route? Step 3: They compare with the Ne and Ar mats and write what arrangement each atom would end up with (e.g. Na after losing 1 electron: 2,8 like Ne; Cl after gaining 1: 2,8,8 like Ar). They also mark which atoms need the fewest electrons moved.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute mats and counters. Say: 'You are the chemists in the 1900s who have just learned about electrons. Your job is to collect data, not to guess.' Model one example on the board: build Na 2,8,1 and ask 'What is left if I take away the one outer electron?' WAIT TIME: 10-15 seconds. Circulate with a checklist and ask each group: 'Show me how many moves Mg needs to lose electrons and how many to gain. Which is fewer?' Prompts: 'What do you notice about the arrangements Na, Mg, O and Cl end with? Compare with your Ne and Ar mats.' Cold-call 2 groups to share their table for O and Cl: 'Kipchoge's group, how many electrons does oxygen need to gain? What does it become like?' Remind groups to include Kenyan connections: 'Chlorine in the water of Nairobi and Mombasa is a Cl atom looking to gain one electron.' Make sure learners record without yet explaining.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Data table and pattern-finding using physical models (Developing and Using Models, SEP 2): moving counters makes the abstract idea of losing or gaining electrons concrete, and the table helps learners compare fewest-moves routes to spot the pattern that atoms end with the noble gas arrangement.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) group tables correctly show Na: lose 1/gain 7; Mg: lose 2/gain 6; O: lose 6/gain 2; Cl: lose 7/gain 1; (2) learners correctly state that the full outer level reached is 2,8 (Ne-like) or 2,8,8 (Ar-like); (3) learners use counters accurately without leaving partial outer rings. Use a thumbs-up check: 'Show me thumbs up if your table agrees with the Ne and Ar mats.' Record groups needing support with counting the outer level, especially distinguishing the full inner levels from the outer one.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to their predictions and use Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) to write a short explanation on a sticky note for one question: 'Why does sodium lose one electron rather than gain seven, and why does chlorine gain one rather than lose seven?' Claim: statement about what each atom does. Evidence: data from their table (outer electrons, electrons to lose or gain). Reasoning: link to the stable noble gas arrangement (full outer level, octet; He duplet). They then explain, in whole-class discussion, why Ne and Ar do not react (already full outer level) while Na and K react vigorously (one electron to lose to reach a stable arrangement). They also tackle O: gains 2 to reach Ne-like arrangement. They revise their original prediction in a different colour pen and note what changed.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Now you have data. Use it. A good explanation has a claim, evidence from your table, and reasoning about stability.' Show a CER frame on the board. Give 4 minutes of individual writing. Ask: 'Why is it easier for sodium to lose one electron than gain seven?' WAIT TIME: 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 4 learners in turn (Wanjiku, Otieno, Amina, Kipchoge as examples): one on Na, one on Mg, one on O, one on Cl. Probe with: 'What does the atom end up looking like?' and 'How does this connect to neon and argon not reacting?' Introduce vocabulary on the board: stable, full outer level, octet (8 outer electrons), duplet (He, 2). Correct misconceptions: 'Atoms do not literally want things; they become more stable with a full outer level.' Say: 'Atoms in the same group, like Li, Na and K, all have one outer electron to lose, so they behave alike even though their masses differ.' Do NOT draw dot-and-cross diagrams or write ion charges in detail; say: 'Tomorrow we will name these charged particles and write their charges.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (Constructing Explanations, SEP 6) combined with whole-class Talk Moves (revoicing, 'who can add on?'): writing a structured explanation forces learners to connect data to the concept of noble gas stability, while discussion lets them refine and challenge each other's reasoning and revisit their initial predictions.
framework.formativeAssessment: Indicators of understanding: (1) the claim states that Na loses 1 and Cl gains 1 electron; (2) evidence cites the table numbers (e.g. 'Na needs 1 move to lose but 7 to gain'); (3) reasoning uses 'full outer level', 'octet' or 'like Ne/Ar'; (4) learners can state He is stable with 2 electrons (duplet). Collect sticky notes and sort into three piles: complete CER, partial (missing reasoning), and misconception. Exit check: ask all learners to hold up 1, 2, 3 or 4 fingers for the number of outer electrons Mg needs to lose to reach a stable arrangement (answer: 2 fingers).

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the class Driving Question Board (DQB) started in Lesson 1. In groups, they review existing questions and place a green dot on any that today's lesson helps answer (e.g. 'Why do Ne and Ar not react?', 'Why do Li, Na and K react alike?'). They write one or two new questions on sticky notes arising from today, such as 'What exactly is the charge when sodium loses an electron?', 'Do all atoms reach a full outer level by losing or gaining?' or 'How does chlorine make Lake Victoria water safe?'. They place new notes on the DQB under 'Stability' or 'Ions' and talk briefly about how they relate to the driving question.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Walk to the DQB with your group. Find a question we have partly answered today.' Give 2 minutes. Ask: 'Which question can we now answer with evidence? Which new question has come up?' WAIT TIME: 10-15 seconds before taking responses. Cold-call 3 groups to read one question aloud and say how the stability idea helps answer it. Sort new questions into themes: 'What are the charged particles formed?' (Lesson 6), 'How many electrons does each element lose or gain?' (Lesson 7), 'How do atoms combine?' (Lessons 8 and later). Say: 'Great questions. Tomorrow we tackle the first of these.' Praise respectful listening to support the Peace value.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board questioning routine: returning to a public record of questions lets learners see their learning progress, notice what remains unanswered and see the path to the driving question, building ownership of the inquiry.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) at least one correctly matched DQB question answered with 'full outer level' reasoning; (2) new questions that move beyond 'why' to predicting charges or formulae (e.g. 'what ion does Mg make?'); (3) every group contributes at least one question; (4) learners listen to and build on peers' ideas without interrupting. Record the number of groups producing questions that link to ion formation as a signal of readiness for Lesson 6.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners gather around the Class Model poster, the 'Electron Arrangement Model'. Using the model from Lessons 3 and 4 (group = outer electrons; period = occupied energy levels; family reactivity), each group suggests one addition for stability. They add: (1) a new box 'Stable arrangement: full outer level (octet 8; duplet 2 for He) as in He, Ne, Ar'; (2) an arrow showing 'few outer electrons (Na 1, Mg 2): tend to lose electrons'; (3) an arrow showing 'nearly full outer level (O 6, Cl 7): tend to gain electrons'; and (4) a note linking to the phenomenon: 'Ne and Ar already stable, so no reaction'. They also note a gap: 'We still need to name the particles formed and their charges' as a Lesson 6 task. Learners copy the updated model into their notebooks and label with a Kenyan example, such as chlorine in Nairobi and Mombasa water treatment.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'A model is a tool to explain and predict. What do we need to add today so our model can explain why Ne is unreactive?' Give 2 minutes for groups to draft their additions on mini whiteboards. WAIT TIME: 10-15 seconds before calling groups. Cold-call 3 groups to propose one addition each; ask the class 'Do you agree? What evidence supports it?' Invite two learners to write the agreed additions on the poster. Ask: 'Does our model yet explain why Li, Na and K react alike?' (yes: same outer electron, same route to stability) and 'Can it predict the charge of the particle formed?' (not yet). Close by pointing to the unanswered gap: 'Tomorrow in Lesson 6 we will predict the ions and draw dot-and-cross diagrams.' Remind them to bring their Element Cards.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision (Developing and Using Models, SEP 2): adding the stability idea to the existing Class Model shows how new evidence refines earlier ideas, and identifying gaps keeps the inquiry moving toward predicting ions and compounds.
framework.formativeAssessment: Indicators: (1) the group proposal correctly states that atoms lose or gain electrons to reach a full outer level like a noble gas; (2) learners link the Class Model to both Ne/Ar unreactivity and the Na/K reactivity; (3) learners identify at least one limitation (cannot yet predict charges). Use a 3-question exit ticket: 'Why is neon unreactive? Will Mg lose or gain electrons and how many? Which noble gas arrangement does Cl reach?' Expected: full outer level; lose 2; Ar-like (2,8,8). Review tickets before Lesson 6.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect: (1) Did learners use evidence from the counter table rather than saying atoms 'want' electrons? Which wording did they use? (2) How many groups correctly identified the easier route (lose 1 for Na, gain 1 for Cl, lose 2 for Mg, gain 2 for O)? (3) Which learners confused total electrons with outer electrons, and what support (colour-coded counters for inner and outer levels) might help? (4) Did the CER frame help quieter learners such as those who rarely speak? (5) Were the cold-calls and WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds spread fairly across the class? (6) Which DQB questions show readiness for ion formation in Lesson 6? Note adjustments to timing, and prepare the Lesson 6 examples (Na+, Mg2+, O2-, Cl-).

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Ne (2,8), Ar (2,8,8) and He (1s2) have full outer levels and do not react. Na (1 outer electron) and Mg (2) can reach a full outer level by losing few electrons; O (6) and Cl (7) can reach it by gaining few electrons. After moving electrons, each atom had the same arrangement as a noble gas.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: A full outer level (octet of 8, or duplet of 2 for He) is a stable arrangement. Atoms with few outer electrons tend to lose them, and atoms with nearly full outer levels tend to gain electrons, so they become stable like noble gases. Atoms in the same group, such as Li, Na and K, behave alike because they have the same outer electron count.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Ne and Ar do not react because their outer levels are already full, whereas Na and K react vigorously because losing one outer electron gives a stable arrangement, and chlorine used in Nairobi and Mombasa water treatment reacts because it needs just one more electron to reach the Ar arrangement. This helps explain why elements in the same group behave alike and why neighbours such as Na, Mg, Ne and Ar differ.

LESSONS.title: Ion Formation: Predicting Cations and Anions and Drawing Dot-and-Cross Diagrams
LESSONS.duration: 40 minutes (one double lesson of 80 minutes may be used for the Model Building Phase)
LESSONS.aresKeywords: ion, cation, anion, electron arrangement, dot-and-cross diagram, noble gas arrangement, s and p notation, Na+, Cl-, Mg2+, O2-

slo.purpose: Learners use the electron arrangements of atoms and the noble gas target from Lesson 5 to predict whether an atom forms a cation or an anion, draw dot-and-cross diagrams of the ions, and write the electron arrangements of the ions in s and p notation. This advances the driving question by showing how outer electron count lets us predict ions.
slo.knowledge: Learners will be able to: (a) relate the position of an element in the periodic table to its electron arrangement and use it to predict the ion it forms; (b) illustrate ion formation of elements (Na+, Mg2+, Al3+, O2-, F-, Cl-, K+, Ca2+) using dot-and-cross diagrams; (c) write the electron arrangement of an ion in s and p notation and state which noble gas it matches (Na+, Mg2+, O2-, F- match Ne; Cl-, K+, Ca2+ match Ar).
slo.skills: Developing and using models (dot-and-cross diagrams); analysing and interpreting data (comparing atom and ion electron arrangements); using mathematics and computational thinking (counting electrons and charges); constructing explanations; engaging in argument from evidence.
slo.attitudes: Learners appreciate the role of electron arrangement in the development of the periodic table. Core competencies: Critical thinking and problem solving (creating new ideas while drawing diagrams of ions using dots and/or crosses to illustrate ion formation); Communication and Collaboration (listening keenly and using open questions while discussing with peers). Value: Peace (showing compassion by displaying tolerance while predicting the type of ion formed from the electron arrangement of elements with peers). PCIs: Life skills (analytical thinking) as the learner predicts the type of ion formed from a given electron arrangement of an atom; Socio-Economic and Environmental Issues (social cohesion) as the learner discusses with peers how atoms acquire stability.
slo.keyInquiry: How does electron arrangement influence the arrangement of elements in the periodic table, and how does it help us predict the ions and compounds elements form? (Today's focus: Which ion will an atom form, and how does the ion's electron arrangement compare with the noble gases Ne and Ar?)
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 5 explained that atoms lose or gain electrons to reach the stable full outer level of noble gases. Lesson 6 turns that idea into predictions: learners work out the exact ion each atom forms, its charge and its new electron arrangement. This gives the ion charges that Lesson 7 (valency and oxidation numbers) and Lesson 8 (formulae) will build on, and it explains why Na and Cl in water treatment and salt behave as they do.
slo.safetyNotes: This is a paper-and-pencil and modelling lesson, so there are no chemical hazards. If a teacher demonstration is used to recall the Na or K reaction with water, use only a video or the teacher's earlier notes; do not let learners handle reactive metals. Use coloured counters or beads carefully (do not put them in the mouth) and keep the floor clear of dropped items.

LESSONS.overview: Mwalimu Achieng recalls the puzzle from the Kisumu class: sodium reacts vigorously with water while neon does not react at all. Learners first predict what happens to a sodium atom (2,8,1) and a chlorine atom (2,8,7) when each moves towards a stable arrangement. They then work in groups of four (Wanjiku, Otieno, Amina and Kipchoge style roles) with counters, dot-and-cross cards and the Element Cards to build ions for Na, Mg, Al, O, F, Cl, K and Ca. They write each ion's electron arrangement in s and p notation and discover that Na+, Mg2+, O2- and F- have the same arrangement as Ne (1s2 2s2 2p6), while Cl-, K+ and Ca2+ have the same arrangement as Ar (1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6). In the Explain Phase learners build a rule: metals with 1 to 3 outer electrons lose them to form cations, and non-metals with 5 to 7 outer electrons gain electrons to form anions. The DQB is updated and the Electron Arrangement Model is revised to include ions.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners look at two Element Cards: sodium (Z11, 2,8,1, 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s1) and chlorine (Z17, 2,8,7, 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p5). They recall that sodium reacts vigorously with water, that Ne and Ar do not react, and that chlorine is used in Nairobi and Mombasa to treat water. Individually they write a prediction in their notebooks: 'What will a sodium atom do with its outer electron, and what will a chlorine atom do, to become like a noble gas? What charge will each have?' They draw a quick sketch of the electron shells and share with a partner. (3 minutes writing, 2 minutes pair share.)
framework.teacherMoves: Display the two cards on the board. Say: 'Yesterday we learned that Ne and Ar are stable because their outer levels are full. Sodium has 1 outer electron and chlorine has 7. Predict: what will each atom do to become stable, and what charge will it carry? Draw it, do not just say it.' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds of silence before learners write. Circulate and note predictions without correcting. Cold-call 3 learners (e.g. Wanjiku, Otieno, Amina) to share their prediction, and ask 'What made you think that?' Record 2-3 different predictions on the board, including incorrect ones (for example 'Na gains 7 electrons'), and tell learners 'We will test these ideas with evidence in a few minutes.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (POE) with elicitation of initial ideas: writing a prediction and a drawn sketch before instruction makes learners commit to a model, exposes misconceptions about whether atoms 'lose' or 'gain' the smaller number of electrons, and creates a reason to look carefully at the evidence in the Observe Phase.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) learners who link the outer electron count (1 and 7) to the noble gas target from Lesson 5; (2) learners who include a charge in the prediction; (3) the misconception that atoms always gain electrons or that the nucleus changes. Tally on a class list how many predict Na loses 1 electron and Cl gains 1 electron. Accept all predictions at this stage and record the tally for comparison after the Observe Phase.

framework.learnerExperience: In groups of four, learners receive an 'Ion Evidence Pack' with coloured counters (dots for one atom, crosses for the other), an electron-shell template and a data table of atoms: Na (2,8,1), Mg (2,8,2), Al (2,8,3), O (2,8,6 i.e. 1s2 2s2 2p4), F (2,7), Cl (2,8,7), K (2,8,8,1) and Ca (2,8,8,2). Step 1: for Na, they place counters on the outer shell, then move the outer electron away and record the number of protons (11) and electrons (10), the resulting charge (1+) and the new arrangement (2,8). Step 2: they repeat for Cl, adding one counter to the outer shell to make 2,8,8, with 17 protons and 18 electrons, giving 1-. Step 3: they complete the table for Mg2+, Al3+, O2-, F-, K+ and Ca2+. Step 4: they write the s and p notation for each ion (e.g. Na+ 1s2 2s2 2p6; Cl- 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6) and circle which noble gas it matches. They also draw dot-and-cross diagrams: a sodium atom with one dot in the outer shell transferring to a chlorine atom with seven crosses, showing the final ions in square brackets with charges, [Na]+ and [Cl]- with 8 outer electrons.
framework.teacherMoves: Model one complete example (Na to Na+) on the board with the group table, showing protons staying at 11 while electrons change from 11 to 10. Say: 'Look at the nucleus. Does the number of protons change? Count again.' Circulate with a checklist. Ask groups: 'How many protons? How many electrons? What is the difference, and what charge does that give?' Use WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after each question before taking answers. Cold-call 2 groups to show their Cl- diagram on the board and ask others to find any error. Prompt groups that are stuck: 'Which noble gas is closest to this atom, and how many electrons do you need to move to reach it?' Remind learners that dots belong to one atom and crosses to the other, that brackets and charges go on the final ions, and that only electrons move; protons stay in the nucleus.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Modelling with manipulatives and data table analysis: moving counters physically represents electron transfer, and the table of protons, electrons and charge lets learners see that charge = protons - electrons. Comparing the ion arrangement with Ne and Ar is pattern recognition that links the new ions to the stable noble gases they learned about in Lesson 5.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) groups correctly count protons and electrons for at least six of the eight ions; (2) dot-and-cross diagrams use dots for one atom and crosses for the other, with square brackets and charges; (3) learners write 1s2 2s2 2p6 for Na+, Mg2+, O2- and F- and 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 for Cl-, K+ and Ca2+; (4) learners do not change the number of protons. Use a quick checklist for each group; give a thumbs-up card for correct tables and ask groups with errors to recheck the electron count.

framework.learnerExperience: Each group studies its completed table and writes a rule in the form: 'Atoms with ___ outer electrons ___ electrons to form a ___ (cation/anion) with charge ___ because ___.' They then use the rule to predict, without counters, the ions formed by Li (2,1), Be (2,2), N (2,5) and S (2,8,6), and check against the group number. Learners explain in a 'claim, evidence, reasoning' format why Na+ and Ne have the same electron arrangement but are different particles (Na+ has 11 protons, Ne has 10). They also explain why Mg2+ needs two electrons to be lost but F- needs only one to be gained, and link back to the puzzle: sodium reacts vigorously with water because its single outer electron is easily lost to reach a stable arrangement, while neon does not react because it already has a full outer level. A final class discussion links chloride ions in Nairobi and Mombasa water and in common salt (NaCl) to the idea that chlorine gains one electron.
framework.teacherMoves: Ask groups to read their rule aloud and ask: 'What evidence in your table supports that rule?' Use WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after the question. Cold-call 4 learners from different groups (for example Kipchoge, Amina, Wanjiku, Otieno) to share and ask others to agree, add on or challenge: 'Do you agree with Kipchoge? What would you add?' Ask the challenge question: 'Na+ and Ne have the same arrangement. Are they the same thing? Why not?' and guide with: 'Think about protons.' Draw out that metals (1 to 3 outer electrons) lose electrons to form cations, non-metals (5 to 7 outer electrons) gain electrons to form anions, and the charge equals the number of electrons lost or gained. Write the class rule on the board and link to group numbers: group 1 gives 1+, group 2 gives 2+, group 13 gives 3+, group 15 gives 3-, group 16 gives 2-, group 17 gives 1-. Avoid introducing bond types; say 'In sub-strand 1.4 we will study how ions and shared electrons hold atoms together.' Do not teach oxidation numbers or valency in detail; say 'Next lesson we will give these charges the names valency and oxidation number.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) with a rule-building discussion: learners build a general claim from the table (evidence) and justify it with the stability idea (reasoning), which turns a set of examples into a transferable predictive rule. The challenge question about Na+ and Ne targets the misconception that the ion becomes the noble gas atom.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) correct predictions of Li+, Be2+, N3- and S2- with reasons stated in terms of reaching a noble gas arrangement; (2) use of the words cation and anion correctly; (3) a clear statement that the number of protons does not change; (4) learners use the group number to predict the charge. Use a 3-question exit slip: (a) Write the ion formed by Ca and its s and p notation. (b) Is Cl- a cation or an anion? (c) Which noble gas has the same arrangement as O2-? Success means at least 2 of 3 correct; those who miss go for a short reteach in pairs at the start of the next lesson.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the class Driving Question Board started in Lesson 1. Each group writes on sticky notes (a) one question that has now been answered, for example 'Why does sodium react but neon does not?', and moves it to the 'Answered' section with a short evidence statement (for example 'Na loses 1 electron to become Na+ 2,8 like Ne'); and (b) one new question, for example 'How do we know the charge to write when making a formula like Al2O3?', 'Why do iron and copper form more than one ion?' or 'What holds Na+ and Cl- together in salt?'. They place the new notes on the DQB under 'Ions', 'Formulae' or 'Bonding'.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Take two minutes with your group. Which of our questions can we now answer, and what new question has today's work raised?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before groups start writing. Cold-call 3 groups to read one note aloud and ask: 'Where on the board does this belong, and which lesson do you think will help us answer it?' Sort the new questions with the class into those answered by Lesson 7 (valency and oxidation numbers, variable oxidation numbers of iron and copper), Lesson 8 (formulae such as NaCl, CaCl2, Al2O3), and sub-strand 1.4 (bonding). Praise good questions and reword vague ones, for example 'Why is the table like that?' becomes 'How does the number of outer electrons decide the ion formed?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board as a public record of growing understanding: moving questions to 'Answered' with evidence, and posting new questions, makes learners track their progress, gives ownership of what to investigate next, and links today's ions to the upcoming lessons on valency and formulae.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) at least one answered note per group includes evidence from the ion table (such as 'Cl- is 2,8,8 like Ar'); (2) new questions refer to charges, formulae or bonding rather than recall; (3) learners place questions in the correct category. Record which groups ask about transition elements (Fe, Cu) or bonding so you can use those questions as hooks for Lessons 7 and 10.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revise the class poster 'Electron Arrangement Model'. In their groups they add a new section called 'Ions' with: (1) a labelled diagram of Na to Na+ and Cl to Cl- with electron arrangements 2,8,1 to 2,8 and 2,8,7 to 2,8,8 (s and p notation shown alongside); (2) a small table linking group number to ion charge (group 1: 1+, group 2: 2+, group 13: 3+, group 15: 3-, group 16: 2-, group 17: 1-); (3) a statement of the revised model: 'Atoms lose or gain electrons to get the same arrangement as the nearest noble gas, forming ions with a charge; the number of protons does not change.' Each group adds one example from Kenya, such as K+ from potassium fertilizers (KNO3) used in Kericho and the Rift Valley, Cl- from chlorine in water treatment at Lake Victoria, or Ca2+ in lime used on farms. They then write in their notebooks a short summary: 'What I observed, what I learned, how I can explain it.'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Our model must now explain why sodium reacts and neon does not, and why elements in the same column form ions with the same charge. Add what today's evidence shows.' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, then allow 8 minutes of group work. Walk around and ask: 'What did you change from yesterday's model and why?' Cold-call 2 groups (for example the groups with Kipchoge and Amina) to present their revised section in 1 minute each, and ask the audience: 'What evidence supports that part of the model? What is still missing?' Highlight gaps to carry forward: the model does not yet show how charges combine to give formulae (Lessons 7 and 8) or how reactions are written (Lesson 9). Remind learners that peace and tolerance in discussions means listening to every group's reasoning, including those who disagree.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision with peer critique: adding ions to the Electron Arrangement Model connects today's evidence to earlier ideas (outer electrons, groups, stability), and the audience critique asks learners to defend model components with evidence, which strengthens explanation of the anchoring phenomenon.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) the revised model shows correct electron arrangements for atom and ion with the proton number unchanged; (2) the group-number to charge table is accurate; (3) the model explains why Na and K (group 1) behave alike by forming 1+ ions; (4) a Kenyan example is linked correctly to an ion. Use a 4-point checklist per group. Collect the notebook summaries and use them to plan the start of Lesson 7.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect: Which learners could predict ion charges from group numbers without counters, and which still needed to count electrons? Did any learners think that Na+ becomes a neon atom, or that atoms change their number of protons? Which dot-and-cross conventions (dots for one atom, crosses for the other, square brackets and charges) caused most errors? How well did the Kenyan examples (potassium fertilizers in Kericho, chlorine in Nairobi and Mombasa) help learners see why ions matter? Were the 10-15 second WAIT TIME pauses respected, and did quieter learners contribute when cold-called? What will you adjust in Lesson 7 so that the link from ion charge to valency and oxidation number is smooth, and how will you use the DQB questions about iron and copper?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Atoms of Na, Mg, Al, K and Ca lose electrons and atoms of O, F and Cl gain electrons. The ions formed have the same electron arrangement as a noble gas: Na+, Mg2+, O2- and F- match neon (1s2 2s2 2p6), while Cl-, K+ and Ca2+ match argon (1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6). The number of protons stays the same.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Metals with 1 to 3 outer electrons lose them to form cations; non-metals with 5 to 7 outer electrons gain electrons to form anions. The charge equals the number of electrons lost or gained, and the group number helps predict it. Dot-and-cross diagrams show the transfer of electrons, with the ions in brackets with their charges.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Sodium reacts vigorously because it easily loses its single outer electron to reach the stable neon arrangement, while neon does not react because its outer level is already full. Chlorine gains one electron to reach the argon arrangement, forming Cl-. Elements in the same group form ions of the same charge because they have the same number of outer electrons, which helps us predict ions of elements we have never worked with.

LESSONS.title: Valency and Oxidation Numbers: What Do Electron Arrangements Tell Us About Charge?
LESSONS.aresKeywords: valency, oxidation number, electron arrangement, outer electrons, cation, anion, variable oxidation number, transition elements, iron, copper, Fe2+, Fe3+, Cu+, Cu2+

slo.purpose: To help learners infer the valency and the signed oxidation number of an element from its electron arrangement, and to discuss why transition elements such as iron and copper show more than one oxidation number.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson, the learner should be able to: (a) relate the position of an element in the periodic table to its electron arrangement by using outer electrons to state valency; (b) illustrate ion formation by stating oxidation numbers (Na +1, Mg +2, Al +3, Cl -1, O -2) from electron arrangement; (c) discuss elements with variable oxidation numbers (Fe 2+ and 3+; Cu 1+ and 2+).
slo.skills: Inferring (valency and oxidation number from s and p notation); analysing and interpreting data (tables of outer electrons and ion charges); developing and using models (revising the Class Model 'Electron Arrangement Model'); constructing explanations; communicating with peers.
slo.attitudes: Appreciate the role of electron arrangement in the development of the periodic table. Show tolerance and compassion (Peace) while predicting ions with peers. Practise analytical thinking (life skills) when predicting oxidation numbers. Core competencies: Communication and Collaboration (listening keenly and using open questions); Critical thinking and problem solving.
slo.keyInquiry: How does electron arrangement influence the arrangement of elements in the periodic table, and how does it help us predict the ions and compounds elements form? (Today: what do the outer electrons tell us about valency and oxidation number, and why do iron and copper not follow a single rule?)
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 6 taught learners to predict cations and anions from electron arrangement and to draw dot-and-cross diagrams (Na+, Mg2+, Al3+, O2-, F-, Cl-, K+, Ca2+). Lesson 7 uses these ion charges to separate two ideas: valency (an unsigned number) and oxidation number (a signed number). It also shows the limit of the outer-electron rule with the transition elements iron and copper. This prepares Lesson 8, where learners use valencies, oxidation numbers and radicals to derive formulae.
slo.safetyNotes: This lesson is paper-based and uses data cards and a short observation task. If Mwalimu Achieng shows samples of rust (iron oxide) or copper wire or copper sulfate crystals, learners handle them only with clean dry hands, do not taste or put them near the face, and wash hands afterwards. Keep any copper compounds away from the mouth and eyes. No heating or open flames in this lesson.

LESSONS.overview: Mwalimu Achieng opens with the anchoring phenomenon: why do Li, Na and K (masses 7, 23 and 39) behave alike, why are Ne and Ar unreactive, and why does chlorine appear in Nairobi and Mombasa water treatment as Cl-? Learners already know from Lesson 6 that atoms form ions with fixed charges. Today they predict, then use Element Cards and a data table to infer valency (how many electrons are lost or gained) and oxidation number (the same number with a sign: + for loss, - for gain). They test the outer-electron rule on Na +1, Mg +2, Al +3, Cl -1 and O -2. Then they meet a puzzle: a Kisumu jua kali metalworker's iron nails and roofing sheets rust to Fe2O3 while iron in FeCl2 behaves differently, and copper forms both Cu+ and Cu2+. Learners discover that transition elements can lose different numbers of electrons, so outer-electron count alone does not predict a single oxidation number. They add this to the DQB and revise the Class Model.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners sit in groups of four (Wanjiku, Otieno, Amina and Kipchoge's group is used as an example). On a slip of paper each learner independently predicts and writes: (1) the charge on a sodium ion, a magnesium ion, an aluminium ion, a chloride ion and an oxide ion, using what they remember from Lesson 6; (2) whether iron might form only one ion or more than one, and why. They write one sentence beginning, 'I think valency and oxidation number are ... because ...'. They then share predictions in their group and agree on one group prediction to record on the board.
framework.teacherMoves: Greet learners and say: 'Yesterday we predicted ions from electron arrangement. Today we ask a sharper question: can we state a charge with a sign, and does every element follow one rule?' Display on the board: Na 2,8,1; Mg 2,8,2; Al 2,8,3; Cl 2,8,7; O 2,6. Say: 'Write your own prediction first. No talking for two minutes.' Circulate silently and note common ideas. Ask: 'Is valency the same thing as charge? Write what you think.' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds after each question before taking answers. Cold-call 3 learners (not volunteers) to read their predictions for Mg and Cl. Cold-call 2 more groups for their prediction on iron. Do not correct answers; record all on the board under the heading 'Our predictions'. Link back: 'Remember our phenomenon: Li, Na and K behave alike. Keep that in mind as we predict.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Eliciting prior ideas (Predict-Write-Share): writing individually before group talk makes every learner commit to an idea, which exposes misconceptions such as 'valency and oxidation number are exactly the same thing' or 'all metals form one ion'. Comparing predictions with later evidence builds conceptual change and ownership.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check slips for observable indicators: (a) learners link ion charge to outer electrons (e.g. 'Mg has 2 outer electrons so Mg2+'); (b) learners attach a sign to the charge; (c) learners give any reasoned idea about iron. Tally on a clipboard how many predicted Cl as 1- and how many wrote 7+. Note learners who assume iron has only one ion for the later discussion.

framework.learnerExperience: Part A (15 minutes in total for the Observe Phase, 8 minutes here): Each group receives a Data Table of Element Cards with columns: element, electron arrangement (energy-level form and s and p notation), outer electrons, electrons lost or gained, ion formed, valency, oxidation number. Rows given: Na (2,8,1; 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s1), Mg (2,8,2), Al (2,8,3), O (2,6), Cl (2,8,7). Learners complete the blanks and notice patterns: Na loses 1 electron, valency 1, oxidation number +1; Mg loses 2, valency 2, +2; Al loses 3, valency 3, +3; O gains 2, valency 2, -2; Cl gains 1, valency 1, -1. Part B: groups receive a second card set for transition elements: Iron: Fe2+ in FeCl2 and Fe3+ in Fe2O3 (rust on roofing sheets and nails in Kisumu); Copper: Cu+ and Cu2+ (CuO). Learners record the oxidation numbers (+2 and +3 for iron; +1 and +2 for copper) and compare these with the single numbers obtained for Na, Mg, Al, Cl and O. They highlight in a different colour where the table breaks the pattern.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute the Data Tables and say: 'Your job as chemists is to find the rule that links outer electrons to valency and to oxidation number. Use your Lesson 6 ion charges.' Model one row on the board (Na): 'Sodium has 1 outer electron. It loses it. How many electrons were lost? The valency is 1. Because electrons are negative, losing one makes the ion positive, so the oxidation number is +1.' Then release groups. Circulate and ask open questions: 'What do you notice about the number of outer electrons and the valency?', 'Why does chlorine have a minus sign but sodium has a plus?' Pause WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds after each question. For Part B, say: 'Look at iron. FeCl2 and Fe2O3 are both real compounds. Which numbers can you write in the oxidation number column for iron? Copper?' Cold-call 4 groups to report one row each (Na, Mg, Al, then Cl or O). Then cold-call 2 groups to report what they noticed about iron and copper. Probe: 'Did the outer-electron rule give us +2 and +3 for iron? What do you think is different about transition elements?' Hand out a short statement: 'Transition elements can lose electrons from more than one energy level, so they can form more than one ion.' Keep the explanation brief; do not teach bonding.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Pattern finding in data tables (Noticing and Wondering): learners compare rows to discover that valency equals the number of electrons lost or gained and that the oxidation number carries a sign. Contrasting main-group data (single numbers) with transition data (multiple numbers) creates a productive puzzle that pushes the rule beyond simple outer-electron counting.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: learners correctly fill at least 4 of 5 rows; they state valency without a sign and oxidation number with a sign; they say aloud that metals give positive and non-metals give negative numbers; they highlight iron and copper rows as exceptions. Use a quick tick sheet. If more than a third of learners write Cl as +7, pause and re-model with the Cl arrangement 2,8,7 needing 1 electron to reach the Ar arrangement.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners work in their groups to construct a written explanation (3-4 sentences) answering: 'How does electron arrangement let us infer valency and oxidation number, and why can iron and copper have more than one oxidation number?' They must use these words: outer electrons, lose, gain, valency, oxidation number, noble gas arrangement, transition element. They then link the explanation to the phenomenon: they write one sentence explaining why Li, Na and K all have oxidation number +1 despite masses 7, 23 and 39, and why Ne and Ar have no oxidation number to predict in this way (full outer level, 8 outer electrons, no tendency to lose or gain). Learners also complete a short application task: state valency and oxidation number for K, Ca, F and N from their arrangements (K 2,8,8,1: valency 1, +1; Ca 2,8,8,2: valency 2, +2; F 2,7: valency 1, -1; N 2,5: valency 3, -3). Finally, pairs use Cl- in water treatment at Nairobi and Mombasa: 'What is the oxidation number of chlorine in chloride, and how did you infer it?'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Now explain it in your own words. Use evidence from your table, not just memory.' Provide sentence starters on the board: 'Because the atom has ___ outer electrons, it ___ electrons, so its valency is ___ and its oxidation number is ___.' Circulate and prompt: 'How do you know that is a loss and not a gain?', 'What would make iron different from sodium?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds after each question. Cold-call 3 groups to read their explanations aloud while the rest listen with the task 'Add one idea you did not include'. Ask a follow-up to a different learner each time: 'Do you agree or disagree with that group? Why?' Highlight Amina's or Kipchoge's group (as examples if they offer strong reasoning) and ask others to build on it. Address misconceptions explicitly: 'Valency is never negative. Oxidation number has a sign.' Clarify that iron has two common oxidation numbers, +2 and +3, and copper +1 and +2, and that for transition elements the outer-electron count alone does not decide which one forms. Conclude: 'The rule works beautifully for main groups; transition elements remind us that atoms are more complex. This is why FeCl2 and Fe2O3 contain different iron ions.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning with peer critique: learners state a claim (valency and oxidation number follow from electron arrangement), cite evidence from the data table (rows for Na, Mg, Al, Cl, O and for Fe, Cu), and give reasoning using the noble gas arrangement. Listening to others and adding ideas builds the Communication and Collaboration competency and shows the limits of a model.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for explanations that (a) correctly state valency as a number of electrons lost or gained; (b) assign the right sign; (c) refer to the stable noble gas arrangement; (d) acknowledge that iron and copper have more than one oxidation number because they are transition elements. Use a 3-point check: 3 = all four elements present; 2 = three; 1 = two or fewer. Collect two exit examples from groups for the 4 K, Ca, F, N answers to verify at least 80% accuracy.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners review the class Driving Question Board started in Lesson 1. In groups they write new questions on sticky notes prompted by today's evidence, such as: 'Why do transition elements lose different numbers of electrons?', 'How do we know which iron ion is in rust?', 'How do we use oxidation numbers to write formulae like Fe2O3 and FeCl2?', 'What other elements have variable oxidation numbers?' They also move previously posted questions that have now been answered (for example 'Why does sodium form Na+?') to an 'Answered' section, with a short note of the evidence. Each group places at least one new question and one answered question on the DQB.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Look at the DQB. Which of our questions did today's evidence help to answer? What new questions has it raised?' Give 3 minutes of silent writing, then 2 minutes of group sharing. Cold-call 4 groups to read one new question and say where it belongs on the board (connected to which part of the phenomenon). Ask: 'Which question will Lesson 8 help us answer?' and point to formula questions. WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before calling on anyone. Highlight any question about formulae and say: 'Next lesson, we will use these valencies and oxidation numbers, together with radicals such as nitrate in KNO3 fertilizer used in Kericho, to derive formulae.' Also remind learners of the link to the driving question: how electron arrangement helps predict ions and compounds.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board tracking: documenting answered and new questions makes learning progress visible and keeps the phenomenon at the centre. Learners see that evidence (the table, the iron and copper puzzle) produces both answers and new questions, which models authentic scientific inquiry.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: each group posts at least one question that is specific to today's content (valency, oxidation number, or variable oxidation numbers); questions are testable rather than yes/no; learners correctly identify at least one answered question and cite the evidence. Note groups whose questions show confusion between valency and oxidation number for follow-up at the start of Lesson 8.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revisit the Class Model poster 'Electron Arrangement Model'. In groups they add today's ideas: (1) next to each group (1, 2, 13, 16, 17), a label giving the usual valency and oxidation number (group 1: +1; group 2: +2; group 13 (Al): +3; group 16 (O): -2; group 17 (Cl): -1); (2) an arrow from 'outer electrons' to 'valency' to 'oxidation number (with sign)'; (3) a boxed note: 'Transition elements (e.g. Fe: +2, +3; Cu: +1, +2) can have more than one oxidation number'. Each group also draws a small labelled sketch for one element, e.g. Mg: 2,8,2 -> loses 2 electrons -> Mg2+ (2,8) -> valency 2, oxidation number +2, same arrangement as Ne. Learners then write in their notebooks: 'The model now explains ... but cannot yet explain ...'.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Our Class Model must explain more than it did yesterday. What new idea do we add and where?' Hand out markers and let each group add one element to the poster (assign Na, Mg, Al, Cl, O, Fe, Cu across groups). Circulate and ask: 'Where on the model does the sign of the oxidation number come from?', 'Which part of the model needs a warning label for iron and copper?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds after each question. Cold-call 3 learners to explain an addition made by another group and say whether they agree. Introduce the 'gap' sentence: 'The model now explains ___ but cannot yet explain ___.' Expected gaps: how to combine ions into formulae and how to use brackets for radicals. Close by tying back to the phenomenon: 'Because Li, Na and K each have one outer electron, each forms +1 and reacts alike; because Cl needs one electron, it forms -1 and is used to disinfect water in Nairobi and Mombasa. Next lesson we use these numbers to write formulae.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision: adding valency, signed oxidation number and the transition element exception to the Class Model connects each new piece of evidence to the full causal chain (electron arrangement -> outer electrons -> group -> ion -> oxidation number). Naming what the model cannot yet explain builds scientific honesty and sets up the next lesson.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: the revised poster shows outer electrons leading to valency and then to the signed oxidation number; the transition element note is present with correct numbers (Fe +2, +3; Cu +1, +2); at least 80% of notebooks contain a correct 'explains/cannot yet explain' sentence. Collect one notebook sentence per group as an exit ticket and use it to plan Lesson 8.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, consider: Did learners distinguish valency (unsigned, whole number) from oxidation number (signed)? Which groups still wrote Cl as +7 or O as +2, and what did their reasoning reveal? How well did learners cope with the iron and copper puzzle, and did any learner claim that all metals form one ion? Were all learners participating in the cold-call routine, including quieter learners? Did the Kenya contexts (rusting roofing sheets in Kisumu, chlorine in Nairobi and Mombasa water) help learners connect the ideas to the phenomenon? Note which DQB questions to carry into Lesson 8, such as formulae for FeCl2 and Fe2O3, and how you will revisit unresolved misconceptions at the start of that lesson.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We observed that Na, Mg and Al lose 1, 2 and 3 electrons to give oxidation numbers +1, +2 and +3, while Cl gains 1 and O gains 2 to give -1 and -2. We observed that iron forms Fe2+ and Fe3+ (in FeCl2 and Fe2O3) and copper forms Cu+ and Cu2+, so these transition elements have more than one oxidation number.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: We learned that valency is the number of electrons an atom loses, gains or shares (a positive whole number), and the oxidation number is the same number with a sign (+ for loss, - for gain). We learned that outer electrons let us infer these numbers for main-group elements, but transition elements such as iron and copper can have variable oxidation numbers.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Elements in the same group, such as Li, Na and K, have the same outer electron count, so they all have valency 1 and oxidation number +1 and react alike despite masses of 7, 23 and 39. Atoms lose or gain electrons to reach the stable noble gas arrangement, which is why Na forms +1 and Cl forms -1. Iron and copper show that the outer-electron rule has limits, and this prepares us to use valencies and oxidation numbers to derive formulae next lesson.
