LESSONS.title: Radicals and Deriving Formulae: Predicting the Compounds Elements Form
LESSONS.duration: 40 minutes (one lesson; extend to a double lesson if learners need more practice)
LESSONS.aresKeywords: radicals, valency, oxidation number, criss-cross method, chemical formula, brackets, nitrate, sulfate, hydroxide, carbonate, ammonium, phosphate, KNO3, NaCl, CaCl2, Al2O3, fertilizer

slo.purpose: Learners use the valencies and oxidation numbers inferred from electron arrangement in Lessons 6 and 7, together with radicals, to derive formulae of compounds. This shows how electron arrangement lets chemists predict the compounds an element forms, such as NaCl, CaCl2, Al2O3 and the fertilizer KNO3.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson, the learner should be able to: (c) derive the formulae of compounds. Learners will know that a radical is a charged group of atoms that stays together (NO3-, OH-, SO4 2-, CO3 2-, NH4+, PO4 3-). They will know that a compound is neutral, so total positive charge equals total negative charge. They will know that the criss-cross method swaps the valencies and writes them as subscripts, with brackets around a radical when a subscript is needed, e.g. Ca(NO3)2.
slo.skills: Using mathematics and computational thinking (NGSS SEP 5): applying the criss-cross method and checking the charge balance. Constructing explanations (SEP 6): explaining why Al2O3 has the ratio 2:3. Developing and using models (SEP 2): revising the Class Model to link electron arrangement to ion charge to formula. Communication and Collaboration: listening keenly and using open questions in pairs.
slo.attitudes: Appreciate the role of electron arrangement in the development of the periodic table (outcome e). Show tolerance and patience with peers while checking each other's formulae (Peace). Life skills (analytical thinking): reasoning step by step from electron arrangement to formula.
slo.keyInquiry: How does electron arrangement influence the arrangement of elements in the periodic table, and how does it help us predict the ions and compounds elements form?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 7 gave the valency and signed oxidation number of each element from its electron arrangement. Lesson 8 takes the next step by combining those ions into neutral compounds, so learners can predict formulae such as NaCl, CaCl2, Al2O3 and KNO3 without having seen them. This prepares for Lesson 9, where the formulae are used in balanced equations, and for Lesson 10, where learners predict SrCl2 and SrO for strontium.
slo.safetyNotes: This is a paper-and-card lesson with no chemicals. If a real fertilizer sample (e.g. KNO3 or ammonium sulfate) is shown, keep it in a sealed container, do not let learners taste or handle it, and have learners wash their hands afterwards. Remind learners that fertilizers are not food.

LESSONS.overview: Mwalimu Achieng opens with the phenomenon. Chlorine compounds treat water in Nairobi and Mombasa, and potassium compounds such as KNO3 feed crops in Kericho and the Rift Valley. How do chemists know the formula of such compounds? Learners predict the formulae of NaCl, CaCl2 and Al2O3 from the ion charges they know. They then use Ion Cards (Na+, Mg2+, Ca2+, Al3+, K+, Fe2+, Fe3+, Cu2+, Cl-, O2-) and Radical Cards (NO3-, OH-, SO4 2-, CO3 2-, NH4+, PO4 3-) to build neutral compounds, testing the charge-balance rule and the criss-cross method. Learners then derive the fertilizer formulae KNO3, K2SO4, Ca(NO3)2 and (NH4)2SO4 and the formulae with variable oxidation numbers (Fe2O3, FeCl2, CuO). They explain the patterns and add 'electron arrangement -> ion charge -> formula' to the Class Model and the DQB. Each of Wanjiku, Otieno, Amina and Kipchoge from the Kisumu class appears in the worked examples.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners recall the Kisumu class phenomenon: Lake Victoria water is treated with chlorine and farms in Kericho use KNO3. Each learner silently writes a prediction on a sticky note or in the notebook: 'Sodium forms Na+ and chlorine forms Cl-. What is the formula of the compound they make, and why?' Then: 'Aluminium forms Al3+ and oxygen forms O2-. Predict the formula of aluminium oxide and explain how many of each ion are needed.' They write one sentence of reasoning and draw a quick sketch of the ions. Typical predictions are NaCl and AlO (a common error), which are used as evidence later.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the question on the board and say: 'Wanjiku, Otieno, Amina and Kipchoge are told that sodium forms Na+ and chlorine forms Cl-. What compound do they make?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds in silence, then 2 minutes of writing. Say: 'Do not worry about being right; I want your best thinking from Lesson 7.' Cold-call 4 learners to read predictions without commenting on right or wrong, and record them in two columns on the board: 'AlO' and 'Al2O3' (and any other ideas). Ask: 'What is your reasoning for the number of ions?' Hold up a 1 cm piece of paper labelled '+' and '-' to show the charges.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Eliciting prior knowledge through individual prediction (Predict-Observe-Explain). Writing before talking makes each learner commit to an idea. The class can then compare their predictions with evidence, which exposes the common error of ignoring charge balance.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check the notes. Indicators: (1) learner correctly names Na+ and Cl- and gives NaCl; (2) learner states the charge on Al3+ and O2- correctly but not the ratio, which is the expected gap; (3) learner mentions that charges must 'cancel' or 'balance' without being prompted. Tally correct NaCl and Al2O3 predictions. Note learners who write AlO or Al3O2 for follow-up in the Observe Phase.

framework.learnerExperience: In groups of 4 (about 8 groups), learners get a pack of Ion Cards (Na+, K+, Mg2+, Ca2+, Al3+, Fe2+, Fe3+, Cu2+, Cl-, O2-) and Radical Cards (NO3-, OH-, SO4 2-, CO3 2-, NH4+, PO4 3-). Station 1: they build NaCl, MgO, CaCl2 and Al2O3 by placing cards side by side until the total charge is zero, and record the number of each ion, e.g. Ca2+ with 2 Cl- gives CaCl2. Station 2: they add the radicals and build KNO3, K2SO4, Ca(NO3)2 and (NH4)2SO4, and notice that brackets are needed when more than one radical is used. Station 3: they build Fe2O3, FeCl2 and CuO using the oxidation numbers from Lesson 7 (Fe3+ with O2-, Fe2+ with Cl-, Cu2+ with O2-). They record each result in a table: ion 1, ion 2, number of each, formula, total charge. They then compare the numbers in each formula with the ion charges and describe any pattern they notice (the number of one ion equals the charge of the other).
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'You are chemists in Kericho deciding what fertilizer to make. Build each compound so that the total charge is zero.' Circulate and ask: 'How many Cl- do you need to balance one Ca2+?' and 'Why did you put brackets around NO3?' For groups who write Al3O2, ask: 'Count the charge. What is 3 x (+3)?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after every question before supporting. Do not give the criss-cross rule yet. Stop the class after 15 minutes and cold-call 3 groups to report one compound each; write the results in a class table on the board: formula, ions, ratio. Ask: 'What do you notice about the numbers in the formula and the charges on the ions?' Record the observations without explaining them.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Gathering evidence with physical models (card building) and pattern finding (SEP 4: analysing and interpreting data). Learners build neutral compounds and see the ratio of ions as a consequence of ion charge, which is a consequence of electron arrangement. The pattern is noticed before the rule is named.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observe whether groups: (1) balance the charge before writing the formula; (2) place brackets around NO3 in Ca(NO3)2 and around NH4 in (NH4)2SO4, but not in KNO3 or K2SO4; (3) get 2:3 for Al2O3 and 1:1 for MgO and NaCl; (4) use Fe3+ for Fe2O3 and Fe2+ for FeCl2. Use a checklist with 8 group names. Groups with 3 of 4 correct are ready for the Explain Phase; others get a guiding question.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners review the class table and explain in pairs why the formulae have the ratios they have, using electron arrangement. They then are introduced to the criss-cross method: write the symbols with their valencies, swap the numbers and write them as subscripts, simplify if possible, and use brackets around radicals when the subscript is greater than 1. They practise: Al3+ and O2- gives Al2O3; Ca2+ and Cl- gives CaCl2; K+ and NO3- gives KNO3; Ca2+ and NO3- gives Ca(NO3)2; NH4+ and SO4 2- gives (NH4)2SO4. They test it on Mg2+ and O2-, which criss-crosses to Mg2O2 and simplifies to MgO, and on Fe3+ and O2- (Fe2O3). Each learner writes a 3-sentence explanation: 'Al2O3 contains 2 Al3+ and 3 O2- because...' Then they complete 6 practice formulae independently: K2SO4, Ca3(PO4)2, Mg(OH)2, Na2CO3, CuO and FeCl3. Finally they link back to the phenomenon: why do Li, Na and K, with very different masses, form similar compounds (LiCl, NaCl, KCl)? Because each has 1 outer electron and forms a 1+ ion.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Turn to your partner and explain why aluminium oxide is Al2O3 and not AlO. Use the word charge.' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, then pairs talk for 2 minutes. Cold-call 3 pairs. Then teach the criss-cross method with the board model: 'Write the ion, swap the numbers, drop the signs.' Emphasise the warning: 'Criss-cross is a shortcut for charge balance, not a replacement for it. Always check that the total positive equals the total negative.' Ask: 'Why do we use brackets in Ca(NO3)2 but not in KNO3?' Pose a challenge: 'What is the formula of calcium phosphate? Predict before we use the method.' Cold-call 4 learners to give the answer Ca3(PO4)2 and check on the board: 3 x 2+ = 6+, 2 x 3- = 6-. Link to the phenomenon: 'Why can a chemist predict the formula of a compound from a group 1 element in any town in Kenya?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Constructing explanations using the claim-evidence-reasoning (CER) structure with a Think-Pair-Share. Claim: the formula of Al2O3. Evidence: the charges on the ions. Reasoning: a compound is neutral and ion charge comes from the electron arrangement. This connects the abstract rule to the underlying cause, which is the electron arrangement and the quest for a stable noble gas arrangement.
framework.formativeAssessment: Collect the 3-sentence explanations and the 6 practice formulae. Success indicators: 5 of 6 formulae correct, with brackets used correctly in Ca3(PO4)2 and Mg(OH)2; the explanation mentions that positive and negative charges balance and that charge comes from lost or gained electrons. Common errors to track: changing subscripts inside a radical (e.g. NO6), forgetting to simplify (Mg2O2), and omitting brackets. Use a traffic-light self-rating (green: correct without help, amber: correct with a hint, red: needs more practice).

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the DQB wall chart started in Lesson 1. Each group writes on sticky notes: (a) one question from this lesson that is now answered, e.g. 'How do we know the formula of potassium nitrate in fertilizers?'; (b) one new question, e.g. 'Why do atoms in NaCl stay together?' (the link to Sub-Strand 1.4), 'What is the formula if the element has two oxidation numbers?', or 'How can we write what happens when sodium reacts with water as an equation?'. They place answered questions in the 'Answered' column with the evidence (the formula, the charge balance) and place new questions on the board under the headings 'Formulae', 'Bonding' and 'Equations'.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Look at the DQB. Which of our questions can we now answer with evidence from today?' WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 3 learners to move one sticky note and justify it. Ask: 'What new question has today created?' Cold-call 2 more learners. Point out that questions on writing equations will be taken up in Lesson 9, and questions on how atoms hold together in NaCl in Sub-Strand 1.4 (Chemical Bonding). Acknowledge each contribution with 'Thank you, that is a good scientific question.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Question tracking with the Driving Question Board. Moving questions from 'open' to 'answered' with evidence makes learning visible and shows that chemistry develops through questions. New questions create a purpose for Lesson 9.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check whether the sticky notes show: (1) at least one answered question linked to specific evidence (e.g. Al3+ and O2- give Al2O3); (2) new questions that go beyond recall, such as asking why or how; (3) correct sorting under 'Formulae', 'Bonding' and 'Equations'. Count the number of groups with both an answered and a new question (target: 8 of 8).

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revise the Class Model poster 'Electron Arrangement Model'. Each group adds to the existing model (electron arrangement -> group and period -> stability -> ion charge -> valency and oxidation number) a new arrow: 'ion charge -> neutral compound formula (charges balance)'. They add a worked example with the element cards, e.g. Ca (2,8,8,2) -> Ca2+ and Cl (2,8,7) -> Cl- -> CaCl2, and one radical example, K+ and NO3- -> KNO3 (fertilizer in Kericho). They write a short caption answering: 'How does electron arrangement help us predict the compounds an element forms?' They then complete the individual Summary Table.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Our model must now explain compounds, not just ions. Where does your new arrow go, and what is it caused by?' WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds. Each group proposes one addition; cold-call 4 groups. Ask: 'Does the model explain why NaCl, KCl and LiCl have the same pattern, even though Li, Na and K have very different masses?' Expect: same outer electron count -> same ion charge -> same formula type. Ask: 'What does the model not yet explain?' Guide learners to the gaps: how atoms share electrons (Sub-Strand 1.4), and how to write equations (Lesson 9). Mark these on the model as 'To be explained'.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision (SEP 2: developing and using models). Adding a link from ion charge to formula extends the model's predictive power, so learners can use it for compounds they have not met. Naming the gaps keeps the model honest.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for models that: (1) show the causal chain from electron arrangement to ion charge to formula; (2) include at least one worked example with correct ions and formula; (3) mention that the compound is neutral; (4) identify at least one gap. Use the Summary Table entries as an exit ticket: the 'explained' column should state that charge balance, which comes from electron arrangement, decides the formula.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, consider: (1) Did learners balance charges first or only follow the criss-cross trick? Look at errors such as Mg2O2 or Al3O2 for evidence. (2) Which learners changed subscripts inside radicals, and do they need a physical card model again? (3) Did the examples with Kericho fertilizers and Lake Victoria water treatment make the link to the phenomenon clear? (4) Were learners able to explain why Li, Na and K form similar compounds despite different masses? (5) What will you adjust in Lesson 9 so learners use today's formulae correctly in balanced equations (e.g. 2Na + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + H2)? Note which pairs worked well together to support peer teaching.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We observed that compounds are neutral, and that ions combine in ratios that balance their charges: NaCl (1:1), MgO (1:1), CaCl2 (1:2), Al2O3 (2:3), KNO3 and Ca(NO3)2 with radicals, and Fe2O3, FeCl2 and CuO for elements with variable oxidation numbers.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: We learned that a radical is a charged group of atoms that stays together (NO3-, OH-, SO4 2-, CO3 2-, NH4+, PO4 3-), and that the criss-cross method, with brackets around radicals when a subscript is needed, helps us derive formulae by swapping valencies and checking that the total positive charge equals the total negative charge.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: We can explain that electron arrangement decides the ion charge (for example, the 1 outer electron of K gives K+, and 3 outer electrons of Al give Al3+). The ion charges then decide how many of each ion are needed to make a neutral compound, so we can predict formulae such as NaCl, CaCl2, Al2O3 and KNO3 and explain why Li, Na and K form similar compounds despite their different masses.

LESSONS.title: Writing and Balancing Chemical Equations: What Happens When Sodium Meets Water?
LESSONS.aresKeywords: word equation, symbol equation, reactants, products, coefficient, balancing, state symbols, conservation of atoms, alkali metals, sodium, potassium, lithium

slo.purpose: To help learners write word and symbol equations with correct formulae and balance them by adjusting coefficients only, using the reactions of group 1 metals with water and other simple reactions as evidence of how outer electron count shapes chemical behaviour.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson, the learner should be able to write balanced chemical equations for simple chemical reactions, including state symbols (s), (l), (g), (aq): 2Na + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + H2, 2K + 2H2O -> 2KOH + H2, 2Li + 2H2O -> 2LiOH + H2, 2Na + Cl2 -> 2NaCl, 4Al + 3O2 -> 2Al2O3 and Ca + 2HCl -> CaCl2 + H2. Learners will also recognise that the same equation pattern fits Li, Na and K because each has one outer electron and forms a 1+ ion.
slo.skills: Developing and using models (writing equations as symbolic models of reactions); analysing and interpreting data (counting atoms on each side); using mathematics and computational thinking (balancing by coefficients); constructing explanations; communicating and collaborating when peers check each other's equations.
slo.attitudes: Appreciate the role of electron arrangement in the development of the periodic table; show precision, patience and tolerance when checking peers' work; value the contribution of scientists in representing reactions with symbols.
slo.keyInquiry: How does electron arrangement influence the arrangement of elements in the periodic table, and how does it help us predict the ions and compounds elements form? (Today: how can one balanced equation pattern describe Li, Na and K, though their masses differ greatly?)
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 8 gave learners the skill to derive correct formulae such as NaOH, KOH, NaCl, Al2O3 and CaCl2. Lesson 4 gave the observation that Li, Na and K react with water with increasing vigour. In Lesson 9 learners combine these to write balanced equations for those reactions, which shows that elements in the same group follow the same equation pattern because they have the same outer electron count. This supplies the final symbolic evidence needed for the Class Model before Lesson 10, where learners predict the position, ion and formula for strontium.
slo.safetyNotes: Do NOT let learners handle sodium, potassium or lithium. Use only a teacher demonstration video or teacher-led demo with a pea-sized piece of sodium, a large trough of water behind a safety screen, learners at least 2 metres back, and goggles on the teacher. Keep tweezers and filter paper for handling; never touch metal with fingers. Store the metal under oil. Have water and a damp cloth ready. If no metal is available, use the video or the reaction description cards. Dilute HCl for the calcium reaction is shown only by the teacher. The hydrogen gas produced is flammable, so keep naked flames away from the demo. Learners wear goggles when near the demo.

LESSONS.overview: Mwalimu Achieng revisits the group 1 water reaction from Lesson 4, in which lithium, sodium and potassium react with increasing vigour despite very different masses (7, 23 and 39). Learners first predict what substances form when sodium meets water and whether the number of atoms stays the same. They then observe a short demonstration or video, collect clues (fizzing, a ball that darts, gas, and a solution that turns red litmus blue), and use their Lesson 8 skills to write correct formulae NaOH and H2. They discover that the unbalanced equation Na + H2O -> NaOH + H2 does not conserve atoms, and balance it using coefficients only: 2Na + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + H2. In groups they then copy the pattern for K and Li and balance other reactions (2Na + Cl2 -> 2NaCl, 4Al + 3O2 -> 2Al2O3, Ca + 2HCl -> CaCl2 + H2) with state symbols. The class adds new questions to the Driving Question Board (DQB) and revises the Electron Arrangement Model (Class Model) to show that the same-group metals follow one equation pattern because each has one outer electron, loses it and forms a 1+ ion.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners sit in groups of four (for example Wanjiku, Otieno, Amina and Kipchoge's group). The teacher recalls the Lesson 4 observations: lithium fizzes steadily, sodium melts into a ball and darts, and potassium burns with a lilac flame. Each learner silently writes on a sticky note: (1) what two new substances they think form when sodium reacts with water, (2) whether the total number of atoms after the reaction will be more, less or the same as before, and (3) whether lithium and potassium will follow the same pattern as sodium, and why. Groups then draw a quick sketch of the reaction in a beaker, labelling Na, H2O and any products they predict. All predictions go on the board unchanged and are revisited later.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'In Lesson 4 we saw sodium dart across water. Today we ask what actually forms, and how chemists write it down.' Show the three metal names Li, Na, K with masses 7, 23, 39. Ask: 'These masses are very different. Will their equations look alike or different? Write your prediction and one reason.' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds of silent thinking before writing. Circulate and cold-call 4 learners from different groups: 'Wanjiku, what product did your group predict? Otieno, why do you think atoms stay the same or change?' Do not correct predictions; say 'Thank you, we will test that.' Record 3 to 4 distinct predictions on the board under 'Our predictions'. Ask groups to hold on to their sticky notes.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Prediction with a reasoning claim (Predict-Observe-Explain): Writing a prediction and a reason before seeing evidence surfaces prior ideas, such as that atoms may disappear in reactions, so the later observation creates a productive conflict that learners must resolve.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observe whether sticky notes name plausible products (a hydroxide, a gas, or hydrogen) and whether learners give a reason that links Li, Na and K to similarity (for example the same column or the same outer electrons). Record how many learners predict atoms are conserved. Indicator: at least half of learners can state a reason for their prediction about whether Li, Na and K follow the same pattern. Note misconceptions such as 'atoms are used up' for use in the Explain Phase.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners observe a teacher demonstration or video of a pea-sized piece of sodium on water in a large trough, then a short clip or description of potassium (lilac flame) and lithium (steady fizzing). Each group completes an observation table with the columns: What we saw, Evidence of a gas, Evidence of a new substance. They note that the metal disappears, the gas is flammable (hydrogen, shown by a lit splint near the gas collected in an upturned test tube, teacher only), and red litmus placed in the final solution turns blue, showing that an alkaline solution forms. The teacher then gives each group a data card: 'Reactants: Na (solid) and H2O (liquid). Products: NaOH (aqueous) and H2 (gas).' Learners write the word equation: sodium + water -> sodium hydroxide + hydrogen. They then write the unbalanced symbol equation Na + H2O -> NaOH + H2 using the Lesson 8 formulae, and count atoms of Na, H and O on each side in a table, finding 2 hydrogen atoms in H2O on the left but 3 on the right (1 in NaOH and 2 in H2).
framework.teacherMoves: Set the safety rules first: 'Everyone stays behind the line. Goggles on. No one touches the metal.' Say: 'Watch and write only what you can observe, not what you think.' Run the demo, pausing after 20 seconds: 'What do you notice? Talk to your partner for 30 seconds.' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before taking answers. Cold-call 3 groups to state one observation each and 2 learners to say which observation is evidence of a gas and which of a new substance. Then hand out the data cards and say: 'Use what you learned in Lesson 8 about formulae to check the formulae NaOH and H2. Why is it NaOH and not NaOH2?' Cold-call 2 learners to justify using the 1+ charge of Na+ and the 1- charge of OH-. Build the atom-counting table on the board with learners calling out numbers. Ask: 'Count hydrogen on the left and right. What do you notice?' Wait 10-15 seconds and cold-call 2 learners. Then say: 'Atoms cannot appear or vanish. What does that tell us about our equation?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Evidence table with claim-evidence pairing and atom-counting: Learners link each observation (gas, alkaline solution, metal disappearing) to a species in the equation, then use an atom inventory to test whether the equation obeys conservation of atoms. This builds the idea that an equation is a model that must match both the evidence and the conservation rule.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that observation tables separate observations from interpretations, and that learners write NaOH and H2 correctly (H2 as a diatomic molecule). Indicator: at least 80 percent of groups produce the correct word equation and the unbalanced symbol equation, and can show on the atom table that hydrogen atoms (and oxygen atoms) are unequal. Listen for learners who say 'the equation is wrong because the numbers do not match'.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners learn the balancing rule: change the coefficients (big numbers in front), never the subscripts. Guided by the teacher, they balance Na + H2O -> NaOH + H2 step by step: (1) put 2 in front of NaOH to give an even number of H on the right? Instead, they test options, find that 2 H2O gives 4 H on the left, then 2 NaOH + 1 H2 gives 2 + 2 = 4 H on the right, which needs 2 Na on the left. The result is 2Na + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + H2, with state symbols: 2Na(s) + 2H2O(l) -> 2NaOH(aq) + H2(g). Groups then use the same pattern to write 2K + 2H2O -> 2KOH + H2 and 2Li + 2H2O -> 2LiOH + H2, and explain why the pattern is the same: each atom has one outer electron, forms a 1+ ion, and combines with OH- in a 1:1 ratio. They then balance three more equations on a worksheet: 2Na + Cl2 -> 2NaCl (related to chlorine used in water treatment in Nairobi and Mombasa), 4Al + 3O2 -> 2Al2O3 (aluminium sufuria surface) and Ca + 2HCl -> CaCl2 + H2. For each, they check their coefficients with an atom table and write which formula came from the ion charges (Al3+ and O2-, so Al2O3; Ca2+ and Cl-, so CaCl2). Learners compare their answers with a partner, then with the board.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Our equation fails the atom count. In balancing there is one rule: change the big numbers in front, never the small numbers inside a formula. Why not? Because changing NaOH to NaOH2 makes a different substance.' Model the first balance aloud with a think-aloud, then say: 'Your turn. Take the potassium reaction and balance it with your partner.' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before groups start and again before taking answers. Circulate with the prompt: 'Show me the atom count on each side.' Cold-call 3 learners to explain one step each and 2 learners to explain why Li, Na and K have the same pattern, expecting the answer 'one outer electron, 1+ ion'. For Al and O2, prompt: 'Use the ions Al3+ and O2- to get the formula first, then balance.' Address the misconception that balancing means editing subscripts by writing 'Al2O3 not AlO' on the board. Finish by asking: 'Why does the mass of the metal not change the equation pattern?' Cold-call 2 learners and affirm answers linking to outer electrons.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Worked example then guided practice with a 'same pattern' comparison (analogy across group 1): Modelling the first balance, then letting learners transfer it to K and Li, builds the idea that group membership, not mass, predicts the form of the equation. The atom table makes the conservation of atoms visible and supports the argument that equations are models of real reactions.
framework.formativeAssessment: Collect whiteboards or worksheets. Indicators: learners balance 2K + 2H2O -> 2KOH + H2 and 2Li + 2H2O -> 2LiOH + H2 without help; they never change subscripts; they include correct state symbols (s), (l), (g), (aq) in at least the sodium equation; and at least two learners per group can explain that Li, Na and K follow the same pattern because of one outer electron. Use a 3-2-1 check: 3 correctly balanced equations is secure, 2 needs support, 1 or fewer needs re-teaching.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the DQB started in Lesson 1. In groups they write new questions or answer existing ones on sticky notes, for example: 'Why does potassium react more vigorously than sodium if the equation looks the same?', 'Why does the equation use H2 and not H?', 'Can we predict the equation for rubidium, which we have never used?', 'How does the electron move when sodium reacts with chlorine in 2Na + Cl2 -> 2NaCl?' Each group moves at least one earlier question to an 'Answered (partly)' area, such as 'What do Li, Na and K have in common?' (same outer electron count, same equation pattern) and 'How do we write the compounds they form?' (formulae from Lesson 8 and now equations). Open questions that point to bonding, for example how atoms share electrons in Cl2, stay on the board as a link to sub-strand 1.4.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Look at the DQB. Which questions can we now answer using today's equations? Which new questions has the balanced equation raised?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds for silent reading of the board. Cold-call 4 learners: 'Amina, choose one question we can now answer and tell us the evidence. Kipchoge, give one new question.' Praise questions that go beyond the lesson. Sort questions into 'answered by evidence', 'partly answered' and 'for later (bonding)'. Ask: 'Which question needs ideas about how electrons move or are shared?' Mark it as a link to the Lesson 10 preview and sub-strand 1.4 without teaching bonding now.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Question-tracking with the Driving Question Board: Moving questions between categories and adding new ones makes learners' growing understanding visible and keeps the phenomenon (same column, same behaviour) at the centre of the inquiry.
framework.formativeAssessment: Count how many groups add at least one new question that connects to electron arrangement (for example about reactivity differences or ion charges in equations). Indicator: each group moves or answers at least one DQB question using evidence from today, such as the balanced sodium equation, and states what evidence supports the answer.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners gather around the Class Model poster 'Electron Arrangement Model'. In groups they add a new panel titled 'Equations as models of reactions'. They draw Na (2,8,1), then Na+ (2,8), and show it joining with OH- in a 1:1 ratio to give NaOH, and write 2Na(s) + 2H2O(l) -> 2NaOH(aq) + H2(g) beneath. They add a note that K and Li follow the same pattern, with K more vigorous because it is lower in group 1, and a note that the Ne and Ar group (full outer level) do not appear in such equations because they do not react. Each learner completes a short exit prompt in their notebook: 'Explain in two sentences why Li, Na and K have equations of the same pattern, and how we know our equation is balanced.' Learners also fill in the summary table for the lesson.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Our model must now explain the symbols we write, not just the electrons.' Ask: 'What should we add to the Class Model so that someone who has never seen our lesson can write the equation for potassium?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, then collect ideas from 3 groups and cold-call 3 learners to read their model panels aloud. Press for the links: 'Where in our model do we show why the coefficient is 2 for Na and for NaOH?' (two atoms each lose one electron). Check that the model avoids teaching bond types. Ask: 'Which part of the model still has a gap?' and note that how atoms share electrons in Cl2 will be explored in sub-strand 1.4. Collect exit prompts and read two aloud anonymously. Preview Lesson 10: 'Next time you will use the whole model to predict the position, ion and formula of strontium, an element you have never worked with.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision with a causal explanation: Adding equations to the Class Model links the invisible cause (one outer electron, loss to form a 1+ ion) to the visible symbolic record (balanced equations), so learners can use the model to predict equations for unfamiliar elements in the same group.
framework.formativeAssessment: Read the exit prompts. Indicators: the learner states that Li, Na and K have one outer electron and form a 1+ ion, so their equations share a pattern; the learner states that balancing uses coefficients to keep atoms equal on both sides; the learner writes at least one balanced equation correctly. Look for the model panel showing 2,8,1 changing to 2,8 for Na+. Learners who attribute the pattern to mass need follow-up at the start of Lesson 10.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect: (1) Did learners separate observation from interpretation during the sodium demonstration? (2) How many learners tried to change subscripts when balancing, and which questioning moved them to change coefficients? (3) Could learners explain that Li, Na and K follow the same equation pattern because of one outer electron rather than their masses? (4) Were the Al and O2 and the Ca and HCl equations too demanding, and who needs extra practice with the atom table before Lesson 10? (5) Which DQB questions about reactivity or electron sharing should be highlighted for the Lesson 10 revisit and the link to sub-strand 1.4? (6) Was the safety routine for the metal demo followed, and would a video be better next time?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We observed that sodium reacts with water by melting into a ball, darting and fizzing, that potassium reacts even more vigorously with a lilac flame and lithium more gently, that a gas (hydrogen) forms and the solution turns red litmus blue. We also saw that the unbalanced equation Na + H2O -> NaOH + H2 has unequal numbers of hydrogen atoms on each side.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: We learned that a chemical equation must have the same number of each kind of atom on both sides, and we balance it by changing coefficients only, never subscripts. We learned to use state symbols (s), (l), (g), (aq) and to write correct formulae first using valencies from Lesson 8.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Li, Na and K have very different masses but each has one outer electron, so each loses it to form a 1+ ion and follows the same equation pattern, 2M + 2H2O -> 2MOH + H2 (for example 2Na + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + H2). The pattern is decided by the outer electron count, which sets the group, and not by mass. Balanced equations for 2Na + Cl2 -> 2NaCl, 4Al + 3O2 -> 2Al2O3 and Ca + 2HCl -> CaCl2 + H2 follow from the ions each element forms.

LESSONS.title: Final Model Revision and Presentation: Using Electron Arrangement to Explain the Periodic Table and Predict Strontium
LESSONS.aresKeywords: electron arrangement, outer electrons, valence electrons, group, period, atomic number, noble gas stability, ion, valency, oxidation number, formula, strontium, Final Explanation, Class Model, DQB

slo.purpose: To bring together everything learned in Lessons 1 to 9 so that learners can write a Final Explanation of the phenomenon, show how electron arrangement fixes an element's group and period, and use the same reasoning to predict the position, ion and formulae of an unfamiliar element, strontium. The lesson ends with a link forward to Sub-Strand 1.4 Chemical Bonding.
slo.knowledge: Learners relate the position of an element in the periodic table to its electron arrangement (outer electrons decide the group, occupied energy levels decide the period). Learners illustrate ion formation as atoms losing or gaining electrons to reach a noble gas arrangement. Learners derive formulae of compounds from ion charges. Learners explain why Li, Na and K (A_r 7, 23, 39) react alike while neighbours such as Na, Mg, Ne and Ar differ.
slo.skills: Constructing explanations from evidence (NGSS SEP 6), developing and using models by comparing the Lesson 1 and final Class Model (SEP 2), engaging in argument from evidence during peer critique (SEP 7), using patterns to make predictions (SEP 4/CCC Patterns), and communicating scientific information orally and in writing (SEP 8).
slo.attitudes: Learners appreciate the role of electron arrangement in the development of the periodic table and the contributions of Mendeleev (1869) and Moseley (1913). Learners show peace and tolerance by listening to and respectfully challenging peers' predictions, and show analytical thinking as a life skill when predicting the ion formed from an electron arrangement. Core competencies: Communication and Collaboration, Critical thinking and problem solving, Learning to learn, Citizenship.
slo.keyInquiry: How does electron arrangement influence the arrangement of elements in the periodic table, and how does it help us predict the ions and compounds elements form? (Forward link to Sub-Strand 1.4: How do chemical bonds influence the properties of substances?)
slo.purposeInStoryline: This is the final lesson of the storyline. In Lesson 1 learners sorted the element cards by mass and met puzzles: Li, Na and K alike, and neighbours very different. Lessons 2 to 9 supplied the pieces (Mendeleev to Moseley and atomic number, electron arrangement, families, stability, ions, valency and oxidation numbers, radicals and formulae, equations). Lesson 10 asks learners to assemble those pieces into one Final Explanation, test it on an element nobody has studied (strontium), complete the DQB, and see what question remains for chemical bonding.
slo.safetyNotes: No chemicals or heating are used. This is a paper, poster and discussion lesson. Learners move around the room to gallery-walk posters, so keep aisles clear of bags. Do not show or demonstrate alkali metal reactions in this lesson; any earlier reaction observations were from video or teacher demonstration only.

LESSONS.overview: Mwalimu Achieng returns to the opening puzzle: sodium, potassium and lithium fizz in water while neon and argon do nothing, and chlorine compounds treat water in Nairobi, Mombasa and from Lake Victoria. Learners first predict where an unfamiliar element, strontium (Z38), would sit and what it would form, using only their own reasoning. They then gather evidence from the whole anchor data set: electron arrangements of the first 20 elements, ion data, and strontium's arrangement 2,8,18,8,2 (1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 3d10 4s2 4p6 5s2). In the Explain phase groups write and present a Final Explanation of the phenomenon, working through Li/Na/K, Na/Mg/Ne/Ar, Cl-, and the Ar 40 versus K 39 mass puzzle. Learners complete the DQB by sorting questions into answered and open (bonding), and finally compare the Lesson 1 Class Model with the final Electron Arrangement Model and write a revised model that includes strontium and previews the octet idea for bonding.

framework.learnerExperience: Mwalimu Achieng displays a single new element card: Sr, atomic number 38, A_r about 88, with no group or period shown. Individually, learners write for 3 minutes: (1) which column of the periodic table Sr belongs in, (2) what ion it will form, (3) the formula of its compound with chlorine, and (4) one sentence of reasoning, referring to the Electron Arrangement Model. They then compare predictions with a partner (Wanjiku with Otieno, Amina with Kipchoge style pairs) and note agreements and disagreements on a sticky note. They also write one sentence: 'The hidden property of atoms that creates the patterns in the table is ______.' This is the same question posed in Lesson 1, answered again with Lesson 1 to 9 knowledge.
framework.teacherMoves: Hold up the Sr card and say: 'Nobody in this class has ever worked with strontium. Chemists in Nairobi or Kisumu laboratories could still predict how it behaves. What would you need to know?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before anyone speaks. Say: 'Write first. I want your own thinking before you talk to anyone.' Circulate and do not correct predictions. After pairs talk, cold-call 4 pairs (not volunteers) to share one prediction and its reason; write each prediction on the board under 'Our predictions' without marking right or wrong. Ask: 'Which prediction used a reason about electrons, and which used a reason about mass?' Point to the Lesson 1 Class Model hung beside the DQB and say: 'In Lesson 1 most of us sorted by mass. Keep that in mind.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Prediction with reasoning (Predict-Observe-Explain). Committing to a written prediction and a reason before seeing data creates a record that learners can revise, making the growth of their thinking visible and giving them a stake in the evidence that follows.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: how many learners give a reason based on electron arrangement or outer electrons versus mass or guesswork; whether any learners already say 'group 2' or 'Sr2+'; whether predicted formulae follow charges (SrCl2 versus SrCl). Record counts on a tally sheet (e.g. 'reason uses outer electrons: __ of __'). Use the tally to decide which step of the Observe phase needs the most support. Learners who give no reason are asked: 'What did you notice about Li, Na and K?'

framework.learnerExperience: In groups of four, learners receive a Whole Evidence Pack on one A3 sheet and use their Element Cards. The pack contains: (a) the table of the first 20 elements with Z, A_r, electron arrangement in energy-level form and s and p notation, group and period; (b) the ion data set (Li+, Na+, K+; Be2+, Mg2+, Ca2+; Al3+; N3-, O2-, F-; P3-, S2-, Cl-) with the noble gas matches (Na+, Mg2+, O2-, F- same as Ne; Cl-, K+, Ca2+ same as Ar); (c) the observations of Li, Na and K with water (Li fizzes steadily and floats; Na melts into a ball and darts; K melts and burns with a lilac flame) and Ne and Ar unreactive; (d) formulae NaCl, MgO, CaCl2, Al2O3, KNO3, K2SO4, Ca(NO3)2, (NH4)2SO4; (e) the new Sr data: Z38, electron arrangement 2,8,18,8,2 and 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 3d10 4s2 4p6 5s2. Learners complete a 'Pattern Finder' table with three tasks: 1. Mark the outer electron count and number of occupied energy levels for Li, Na, K, Mg, Ca and Sr, and state the group and period of each. 2. Find the noble gas whose arrangement matches each ion. 3. Use Ca and Mg to forecast what Sr's outer electrons, group and ion will be, and write the matching row for Sr in the table. They also place the Ar (A_r 40) and K (A_r 39) cards in order and say what decides the order.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute packs and say: 'You are the chemists with all the evidence. Do not look for answers I am hiding. Look for patterns that hold for every element in the pack.' Circulate with three prompt questions: 'How many energy levels does Sr have, counting 2,8,18,8,2?' (five, so period 5); 'How many outer electrons, and what does that say about its group?' (two, group 2, like Mg and Ca); 'Which noble gas arrangement would Sr+2 match?' (krypton-like 2,8,18,8; accept 'the noble gas before it' if Kr has not been named, and note that Kr is Z36, outside the first 20 elements). If a group claims Sr is group 5 because it has five levels, ask: 'Does the number of levels give the group or the period?' and WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 3 groups to state how they found Sr's group and period. Ask all groups: 'Ar has a bigger A_r than K but comes before it. What decides the order?' Cold-call 2 learners; expect 'atomic number, Moseley 1913, not mass as Mendeleev used in 1869'.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Pattern analysis with structured data table (Analyzing and Interpreting Data, NGSS SEP 4; Patterns CCC). Having learners look for patterns that hold across the entire data set, then extend the pattern to Sr, shows them that the rules are general and predictive rather than facts to memorise.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check each group's Pattern Finder for: Sr outer electrons = 2, group 2, period 5; Sr ion = Sr2+; ion matched to a noble gas arrangement; group read from outer electrons and period from levels (not swapped). Observable indicators: learners point to the 5s2 end of the notation and say 'outer level'; they use Mg and Ca as comparison rows. Common errors to note: counting 3d10 electrons as outer electrons; using A_r 88 to decide the group; writing Sr2- for the ion. Note names of groups needing re-teaching and pair them with a stronger group in the Explain phase.

framework.learnerExperience: Part A (20 min): Each group writes a Final Explanation on a poster using a four-box frame. Box 1, ORDER: what decides the order of elements in the periodic table (atomic number, Moseley), how outer electrons decide group and occupied levels decide period. Box 2, SAME COLUMN, DIFFERENT MASS: why Li, Na and K (A_r 7, 23, 39) each have 1 outer electron and react alike with water, with reactivity increasing Li < Na < K; and why neighbours such as Na, Mg, Ne and Ar differ because their outer electron counts differ (1, 2, 8, 8). Box 3, STABILITY AND IONS: why Ne and Ar do not react (full outer level), why Na loses 1 electron to form Na+ (2,8 like Ne), why chlorine gains 1 to form Cl- (2,8,8 like Ar), and how this gives NaCl, CaCl2 and Al2O3, including KNO3 fertilizer used in Kericho and the Rift Valley and chlorine used to treat water in Nairobi, Mombasa and from Lake Victoria. Box 4, PREDICTION: Sr position (group 2, period 5), ion (Sr2+ after losing 2 electrons), formulae SrCl2 and SrO, and the balanced equation Sr + 2HCl -> SrCl2 + H2 written by analogy with Ca + 2HCl -> CaCl2 + H2 (with state symbols (s), (aq), (g)). Part B (15 min): Gallery walk and peer critique. Each group sends 1 presenter to stay and 3 visitors to rotate every 4 minutes with a 'Two Stars and a Wish' critique card, using the criteria: uses evidence, links outer electrons to group, uses the noble gas target to explain the ion, and predicts Sr correctly. Part C (5 min): Forward link. Learners write one question about how atoms share electrons, for example how chlorine atoms stay together as Cl2 or why NaCl differs from other substances. The teacher names this as the focus of Sub-Strand 1.4 Chemical Bonding.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Your Final Explanation must answer the phenomenon question without using the word because alone. Show me the chain: electron arrangement, then outer electrons, then group, then behaviour.' Model the first link only: 'Sodium is 2,8,1. One outer electron means group 1.' Then step back. While circulating, ask: 'If it is mass that mattered, why would Li and K behave alike?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Ask: 'Why does Mg form Mg2+ and not Mg+?' Cold-call 3 learners during Part A to explain one box aloud. Make sure the explanation includes how Sr2+ is reached, not just stated. During the gallery walk, stand at two posters and listen for explanations that confuse valency with oxidation number; remind: 'valency is a positive whole number; oxidation number has a sign.' Listen for any claim that atoms 'want' electrons and respond: 'What does it mean in terms of the arrangement of the electrons and the full outer level?' After the walk, cold-call 4 groups to share the one improvement they will make to their poster and allow 3 minutes for revisions. For Part C, say: 'In Lesson 5 we saw stability comes from a full outer level. In bonding, atoms that cannot easily lose or gain electrons will share them. That is the next unit; hold your question for the DQB.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning with peer critique (Constructing Explanations, NGSS SEP 6; Engaging in Argument from Evidence, SEP 7). Learners build each statement as claim, data from the evidence pack and a reason in terms of electron arrangement, then test it against peers' feedback. Writing the explanation as a cause-and-effect chain (Cause and Effect CCC) shows that electron arrangement is the underlying mechanism.
framework.formativeAssessment: Use a four-item rubric on each poster (0 to 2 points each, 8 total): (1) states that order is by atomic number and not mass; (2) links outer electrons to group and levels to period; (3) explains Li/Na/K likeness and Na/Mg/Ne/Ar differences by outer electrons; (4) predicts Sr correctly (group 2, period 5, Sr2+, SrCl2, SrO) with a reason using the noble gas arrangement. Success: 6 or more out of 8. Observable indicators: learners use the words 'outer electrons' and 'noble gas arrangement' in speech; critique cards cite evidence from the pack. Misconceptions to log: mass decides group; atoms 'want' electrons; Sr+ formed; subscripts changed to balance equations. Collect posters for the record.

framework.learnerExperience: The class gathers at the DQB, which has been growing since Lesson 1. Each group receives 4 to 5 question strips from the board (assigned by the teacher). They sort their questions into three columns: ANSWERED (give the answer in one sentence using electron arrangement and the lesson where it was learned), PARTLY ANSWERED (what is still missing), and NEW/OPEN (questions for chemical bonding, such as how atoms share electrons or how bonds affect properties of substances). Learners add at least one new question strip from the forward-link question written in Part C, and move answered strips to the 'Answered' side with a green dot. They then co-write on a large paper the answer to the main driving question: 'How does electron arrangement influence the arrangement of elements in the periodic table, and how does it help us predict the ions and compounds elements form?' in two sentences.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Let us go back to the questions we asked on Day One. Which ones can we now answer, and which ones will we carry to the next unit?' Hand out strips, give 5 minutes for group sorting, then cold-call 5 groups (one per column or question) to read a strip and give its answer with evidence. For each answer ask: 'Which lesson gave you that evidence?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before accepting a response. Challenge vague answers: 'Say it using outer electrons.' For open questions, ask: 'Why can the periodic table not fully answer this? What do we need to know about how atoms join?' Then pin the forward-link key inquiry question 'How do chemical bonds influence the properties of substances?' on the DQB as the bridge to Sub-Strand 1.4. Praise respectful disagreement to model the value of peace and tolerance, saying: 'Thank you for disagreeing politely with evidence.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board review (question-driven sensemaking). Returning to learners' own questions shows how far understanding has moved and turns unanswered questions into a purpose for the next unit, which sustains curiosity and ownership of learning.
framework.formativeAssessment: Count and record the proportion of strips moved to ANSWERED and check the accuracy of each stated answer. Observable indicators: learners cite lessons (for example 'Lesson 6, Na+ is like Ne'); answers use outer electrons and not mass; new questions are about sharing or joining of atoms, showing readiness for bonding. Note any strips placed in ANSWERED with a wrong or incomplete answer and correct them immediately at the board. The two-sentence class answer to the driving question is checked against the outcome: order by atomic number; outer electrons decide group; levels decide period; stability explains ions and formulae.

framework.learnerExperience: Individually, learners compare the Lesson 1 version of the Class Model (the 'Electron Arrangement Model' poster, then showing sorting mainly by mass and properties, with puzzles marked) with the current version. In pairs they complete a Model Comparison table with two columns, 'Lesson 1 model' and 'Final model', and rows: What decides the order? What explains the same column? What explains neighbours' differences? Why are Ne and Ar unreactive? How do we predict ions? How do we predict formulae? What can we predict about a new element? As a class they then revise the poster: add Sr in group 2, period 5 with 2,8,18,8,2 and the s and p notation ending 5s2; add arrows from outer electrons to group, levels to period, stability to ion charge, ion charge to formula (SrCl2, SrO, CaCl2, NaCl, Al2O3, KNO3); add a 'Next: bonding' box showing atoms that share electrons to reach a full outer level (octet rule preview only; no bond types taught). Each learner writes an individual Final Explanation paragraph (6 to 8 sentences) and completes an exit ticket on a new unfamiliar example: 'Predict the group, ion and formula with chlorine for barium (Z56, outer electrons 2) or for gallium, and explain with outer electrons.'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Put your Lesson 1 sheet beside today's model. What has changed in how you think? Point to one thing you had wrong or missing.' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 4 learners to name one specific change to the model (for example 'mass was not enough; atomic number decides order'). Build the class poster by asking each of 5 pairs to add one revision and justify it with evidence from the pack. Ask: 'Where on this model would we place a bond? Which part is still missing?' Lead learners to see that the model explains why atoms form ions but not yet how atoms that share electrons stay joined. Do not teach bond types; say only 'bonding in Sub-Strand 1.4 will explain this'. Collect exit tickets and read two aloud (anonymously) for the class to check. Close by thanking Mendeleev's and Moseley's work: 'Scientists in 1869 and 1913 built this table without knowing how electrons are arranged; today you used electron arrangement to explain it and predict an element you had never studied.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision with before-and-after comparison (Developing and Using Models, NGSS SEP 2). FINAL_EXPLANATION.instructions: You have finished all 10 lessons on the Periodic Table. Now write your own complete explanation of the driving question: How does electron arrangement influence the arrangement of elements in the periodic table, and how does it help us predict the ions and compounds elements form? Use your Element Cards, your notes from each lesson, the Driving Question Board (DQB) and your Class Model (the Electron Arrangement Model) from Lesson 1 to Lesson 10. Write in complete sentences, use scientific words correctly (atomic number, outer electrons, group, period, noble gas, cation, anion, valency, oxidation number, radical), and give evidence from the activities to support every claim. Show your reasoning clearly: say what you saw, then explain why. Write your answers in the space under each prompt. Take your time and show what you have learned.

sections.title: Part 1: How Is the Periodic Table Ordered?
sections.prompt: In Lesson 1 you sorted the first 20 Element Cards by mass and by properties. (a) Explain how Mendeleev (1869) and Moseley (1913) each ordered the elements. (b) Use the masses and atomic numbers of Ar and K from your Element Cards, and what you know about how each reacts, to explain why the modern table is ordered the way it is. (c) Define a group and a period, and describe where Li, Na and K and where Ne and Ar fell when you arranged the cards by atomic number. (d) Look at the masses of Li, Na and K on your cards, and at Ca and Ar. Why was mass alone not enough to explain the patterns you saw?
sections.exemplar: (a) Mendeleev in 1869 arranged the elements by increasing atomic mass and left gaps for elements that had not yet been discovered. Moseley in 1913 showed that atomic number is the true basis of order. (b) Ar has Z 18 and A_r 40, while K has Z 19 and A_r 39. If we ordered by mass, K would come before Ar. But Ar behaves like Ne (unreactive) and K behaves like Li and Na (reactive), so they only fit their families when ordered by atomic number. This is why the modern table uses atomic number. (c) A group is a vertical column and a period is a horizontal row. When I arranged the cards by atomic number into 4 periods, Li, Na and K fell in one column (group 1), and Ne and Ar fell together in the noble gas column (group 18). (d) Li, Na and K have very different masses (7, 23 and 39) but behave alike, and Ca has the same A_r as Ar (40) but sits in a different group. So mass cannot explain the pattern. Something hidden inside the atom must decide where an element belongs and how it behaves, and this led us to electron arrangement.

sections.title: Part 2: Electron Arrangement, Group and Period
sections.prompt: (a) Write the electron arrangement of each of these atoms in both energy-level form and s and p notation: Li, Na, Cl, Ca. (b) State the rule that links the electron arrangement to the group number for groups 1 and 2 and for groups 13 to 18, and the rule that links it to the period number. Say what is special about He. (c) Use these rules to state the group and period of Na, Cl and Ne. (d) Use your answers to explain why Li, Na and K sit in the same column although their masses are very different, and why neighbours such as Na and Mg do not behave alike.
sections.exemplar: (a) Li: 2,1 and 1s2 2s1. Na: 2,8,1 and 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s1. Cl: 2,8,7 and 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p5. Ca: 2,8,8,2 and 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2. (b) The number of outer electrons decides the group: for groups 1 and 2 the group number equals the number of outer electrons, and for groups 13 to 18 the group number is the number of outer electrons plus 10 (so groups 13 to 18 have 3 to 8 outer electrons). The number of occupied energy levels is the period number. He (1s2) is a special case: it has 2 outer electrons, which fill its only energy level, so it is placed in group 18 with the noble gases rather than in group 2. (c) Na has 1 outer electron and 3 occupied energy levels, so it is in group 1, period 3. Cl has 7 outer electrons and 3 occupied levels, so it is in group 17 (7 + 10), period 3. Ne (2,8) has 8 outer electrons and 2 occupied levels, so it is in group 18 (8 + 10), period 2. (d) Li (2,1), Na (2,8,1) and K (2,8,8,1) each have 1 outer electron, so they are all in group 1 even though their masses are 7, 23 and 39. Na has 1 outer electron but Mg (2,8,2) has 2, so they are in different groups and behave differently. Electron arrangement, which follows from atomic number, is the hidden property that decides the position of an element in the periodic table.

sections.title: Part 3: Families, Stability and Reactivity
sections.prompt: (a) Name the family of each: Li, Mg, Cl and Ar, and give the number of outer electrons of each family. (b) Describe what you saw when Li, Na and K were added to water, and state the reactivity trend down group 1. (c) Use the electron arrangements of Ne (2,8), Ar (2,8,8), Na and Cl to explain why Ne and Ar do not react while Na reacts vigorously and chlorine is used for water treatment in Nairobi and Mombasa.
sections.exemplar: (a) Li is an alkali metal (group 1, 1 outer electron). Mg is an alkaline earth metal (group 2, 2 outer electrons). Cl is a halogen (group 17, 7 outer electrons). Ar is a noble gas (group 18, full outer level of 8 electrons). (b) Li fizzed steadily and floated. Na melted into a ball, darted about and fizzed fast. K melted, burned with a lilac flame and was very vigorous. Reactivity increases down the group: Li < Na < K. (c) Ne and Ar have full outer levels (an octet), which is a stable arrangement, so they do not react. Na has only 1 outer electron, so by losing it, it reaches the stable arrangement of Ne (2,8). It loses 1 electron instead of gaining 7 because that is far easier. Cl has 7 outer electrons, so gaining just 1 electron gives it the Ar arrangement (2,8,8), which is why chlorine reacts easily and can be used to disinfect water in Nairobi and Mombasa. Atoms react to reach a full outer level like a noble gas.

sections.title: Part 4: Predicting Ions, Valency and Formulae
sections.prompt: (a) For each of Na, Mg, Al, O and Cl, write the ion formed with its charge and its electron arrangement in s and p notation, and state which noble gas arrangement it matches. (b) What is the oxidation number of Na, Mg, Al, Cl and O? Explain how it differs from valency. (c) Use the criss-cross method to derive the formulae of calcium chloride, aluminium oxide, and the fertilizer made from potassium and the nitrate radical, used on farms in Kericho and the Rift Valley. Use your Radical Cards from Lesson 8. (d) Why can outer electron count alone not predict the ion of iron or copper? Use the compounds from Lesson 7 as evidence.
sections.exemplar: (a) Na+ is 1s2 2s2 2p6 and matches Ne. Mg2+ is 1s2 2s2 2p6 and matches Ne. Al3+ is 1s2 2s2 2p6 and matches Ne. O2- is 1s2 2s2 2p6 and matches Ne. Cl- is 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 and matches Ar. (b) Na +1, Mg +2, Al +3, Cl -1, O -2. Valency is the number of electrons an atom loses, gains or shares and is always a positive whole number, while the oxidation number is the same number with a sign: + for loss and - for gain. (c) Calcium chloride: Ca2+ and Cl-, criss-cross gives CaCl2. Aluminium oxide: Al3+ and O2- gives Al2O3. Potassium nitrate: K+ and the nitrate radical NO3- give KNO3. In each, the total positive charge equals the total negative charge so the compound is neutral. (d) Iron and copper are transition elements that can lose different numbers of electrons. Iron forms Fe2+ in FeCl2 and Fe3+ in Fe2O3, so it has two oxidation numbers (+2 and +3). Copper forms Cu2+ in CuO and can also form Cu+, so it also has more than one oxidation number (+1 and +2). The outer-electron rule alone therefore does not predict a single oxidation number for these elements.

sections.title: Part 5: Putting It All Together and Predicting Strontium
sections.prompt: Strontium (Sr, Z38) is an element you have never worked with. Its electron arrangement is 2,8,18,8,2. (a) Use this arrangement and the rules you have built to predict its group and period, and explain how you decided. (b) Predict the ion it forms and the formulae of its compounds with chlorine and oxygen. (c) Write a balanced equation with state symbols for sodium reacting with water, and explain why potassium and lithium follow the same pattern. (d) Write a final explanation of the driving question: how does electron arrangement influence the arrangement of elements in the periodic table, and how does it help us predict the ions and compounds they form?
sections.exemplar: (a) Sr has 2 outer electrons (the last number in 2,8,18,8,2) and 5 occupied energy levels (five numbers), so it is in group 2, period 5. (b) It loses 2 electrons to form Sr2+, with a noble gas arrangement like Mg2+ and Ca2+. Criss-cross with Cl- gives SrCl2 and with O2- gives SrO. (c) 2Na(s) + 2H2O(l) -> 2NaOH(aq) + H2(g). Li and K each have 1 outer electron like Na, so each loses it to form a 1+ ion and follows the same pattern: 2K + 2H2O -> 2KOH + H2 and 2Li + 2H2O -> 2LiOH + H2. The pattern depends on the outer electron count, not on mass (7, 23 and 39). (d) Elements are ordered by atomic number, as Moseley showed, and atomic number gives the electron arrangement. The number of outer electrons decides the group and the number of occupied energy levels decides the period. Elements in the same group, such as Li, Na and K, have the same outer electron count so they react alike despite different masses, while neighbours such as Na, Mg, Ne and Ar differ because their outer electron counts differ. Atoms lose or gain electrons to reach the stable noble gas arrangement. This is why Ne and Ar are unreactive, group 1 metals form 1+ ions and chlorine forms Cl-. Knowing the ion charges lets us predict valencies and formulae such as NaCl, CaCl2, Al2O3 and KNO3 for any element, including ones we have never worked with. How atoms share electrons is explained in Sub-Strand 1.4, Chemical Bonding.

SUMMARY_TABLE.drivingQuestion: DRIVING QUESTION: How does electron arrangement influence the arrangement of elements in the periodic table, and how does it help us predict the ions and compounds elements form?

lessons.title: Sorting the Element Cards and Launching the DQB
lessons.observed: We sorted the first 20 Element Cards (H to Ca) by properties and by mass. We saw that Li, Na and K, with very different masses (7, 23, 39), all react with water, with the reaction getting stronger from Li to K, while Ne and Ar do not react at all. We noted that chlorine is used to treat water in Nairobi and Mombasa, and that Ar (A_r 40) is heavier than K (A_r 39) although it comes first.
lessons.learned: Elements can be sorted by properties and by mass into patterns, but mass alone does not explain why some elements of very different mass behave alike while neighbouring elements behave very differently. Mendeleev and Moseley faced this puzzle, and something hidden inside atoms must decide where an element belongs and how it behaves.
lessons.explained: Our first ideas: a hidden property of atoms, possibly linked to electrons, may explain why Li, Na and K are alike and why Ne and Ar are unreactive. We do not yet know what it is. We started the DQB with the driving question and our own questions, and drew the first version of the Class Model, the 'Electron Arrangement Model', to be revised in each lesson.

lessons.title: From Mendeleev's Gaps to Moseley's Atomic Number: Building Groups and Periods
lessons.observed: When the first 20 Element Cards were arranged by atomic number into 4 periods (rows) and groups (columns), Li, Na and K fell in one column and He, Ne and Ar in another. Ar (Z18, A_r 40) had to be placed before K (Z19, A_r 39), and Ca (A_r 40) had the same A_r as Ar but sat in a different group.
lessons.learned: Mendeleev (1869) ordered elements by atomic mass and left gaps for undiscovered elements. Moseley (1913) showed that atomic number is the true basis of order, and the modern table uses atomic number. A group is a vertical column and a period is a horizontal row.
lessons.explained: Mass ordering fails for Ar and K, but atomic number gives a consistent order. The table places elements that behave alike, such as Li, Na and K, in the same group even though their masses differ. The hidden property that causes these patterns is still to be explained and will be explored in Lesson 3.

lessons.title: Writing Electron Arrangements: Reading Group and Period from s and p Notation
lessons.observed: We built the electron arrangements of H to Ca using counters and wrote them in energy-level form (e.g. Na 2,8,1) and s and p notation (e.g. Na 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s1). We noticed that Li (2,1), Na (2,8,1) and K (2,8,8,1) each have 1 outer electron, and that Ne (2,8) and Ar (2,8,8) have full outer levels.
lessons.learned: Group number is decided by the number of outer electrons (group 1 and 2 = number of outer electrons; groups 13 to 18 = outer electrons + 10, with He, 1s2, in group 18). Period number equals the number of occupied energy levels. Elements in the same group have the same outer electron count even though their masses differ.
lessons.explained: Li, Na and K sit in the same column despite masses of 7, 23 and 39 because each atom has 1 outer electron, while neighbours such as Na and Mg differ because their outer electron counts differ (1 and 2). Electron arrangement, the hidden property that follows from atomic number, therefore decides where an element is placed in the periodic table. We still need to explain why outer electrons control how elements react.

lessons.title: Chemical Families and Reactivity Patterns: Why Li, Na and K Behave Alike
lessons.observed: Li fizzes steadily and floats; Na melts into a ball, darts and fizzes fast; K melts, burns with a lilac flame and is very vigorous. Ca reacts faster than Mg. Ne and Ar do not react. Cl and F compounds are used in water treatment in Nairobi and Mombasa. Fe and Cu form more than one ion.
lessons.learned: Elements fall into families: alkali metals (group 1, 1 outer electron), alkaline earth metals (group 2, 2 outer electrons), halogens (group 17, 7 outer electrons), noble gases (group 18, full outer level) and transition elements (between group 2 and 13 from period 4). Reactivity of alkali metals increases down the group: Li < Na < K.
lessons.explained: Elements in the same family behave alike because they have the same number of outer electrons, not the same mass (Li 7, Na 23 and K 39 all have 1 outer electron). Neighbours such as Na and Mg or Na and Ne differ because their outer electron counts differ. Why a full outer level makes Ne and Ar unreactive is still to be explained in Lesson 5.

lessons.title: Stability of Atoms: Why Atoms Lose or Gain Electrons
lessons.observed: Ne (2,8), Ar (2,8,8) and He (1s2) have full outer levels and do not react. Na (1 outer electron) and Mg (2) can reach a full outer level by losing few electrons; O (6) and Cl (7) can reach it by gaining few electrons. After moving electrons, each atom had the same arrangement as a noble gas.
lessons.learned: A full outer level (octet of 8, or duplet of 2 for He) is a stable arrangement. Atoms with few outer electrons tend to lose them, and atoms with nearly full outer levels tend to gain electrons, so they become stable like noble gases. Atoms in the same group, such as Li, Na and K, behave alike because they have the same outer electron count.
lessons.explained: Ne and Ar do not react because their outer levels are already full, whereas Na and K react vigorously because losing one outer electron gives a stable arrangement, and chlorine used in Nairobi and Mombasa water treatment reacts because it needs just one more electron to reach the Ar arrangement. This helps explain why elements in the same group behave alike and why neighbours such as Na, Mg, Ne and Ar differ.

lessons.title: Ion Formation: Predicting Cations and Anions and Drawing Dot-and-Cross Diagrams
lessons.observed: Atoms of Na, Mg, Al, K and Ca lose electrons and atoms of O, F and Cl gain electrons. The ions formed have the same electron arrangement as a noble gas: Na+, Mg2+, O2- and F- match neon (1s2 2s2 2p6), while Cl-, K+ and Ca2+ match argon (1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6). The number of protons stays the same.
lessons.learned: Metals with 1 to 3 outer electrons lose them to form cations; non-metals with 5 to 7 outer electrons gain electrons to form anions. The charge equals the number of electrons lost or gained, and the group number helps predict it. Dot-and-cross diagrams show the transfer of electrons, with the ions in brackets with their charges.
lessons.explained: Sodium reacts vigorously because it easily loses its single outer electron to reach the stable neon arrangement, while neon does not react because its outer level is already full. Chlorine gains one electron to reach the argon arrangement, forming Cl-. Elements in the same group form ions of the same charge because they have the same number of outer electrons, which helps us predict ions of elements we have never worked with.

lessons.title: Valency and Oxidation Numbers: What Do Electron Arrangements Tell Us About Charge?
lessons.observed: We observed that Na, Mg and Al lose 1, 2 and 3 electrons to give oxidation numbers +1, +2 and +3, while Cl gains 1 and O gains 2 to give -1 and -2. We observed that iron forms Fe2+ and Fe3+ (in FeCl2 and Fe2O3) and copper forms Cu+ and Cu2+, so these transition elements have more than one oxidation number.
lessons.learned: We learned that valency is the number of electrons an atom loses, gains or shares (a positive whole number), and the oxidation number is the same number with a sign (+ for loss, - for gain). We learned that outer electrons let us infer these numbers for main-group elements, but transition elements such as iron and copper can have variable oxidation numbers.
lessons.explained: Elements in the same group, such as Li, Na and K, have the same outer electron count, so they all have valency 1 and oxidation number +1 and react alike despite masses of 7, 23 and 39. Atoms lose or gain electrons to reach the stable noble gas arrangement, which is why Na forms +1 and Cl forms -1. Iron and copper show that the outer-electron rule has limits, and this prepares us to use valencies and oxidation numbers to derive formulae next lesson.

lessons.title: Radicals and Deriving Formulae: Predicting the Compounds Elements Form
lessons.observed: We observed that compounds are neutral, and that ions combine in ratios that balance their charges: NaCl (1:1), MgO (1:1), CaCl2 (1:2), Al2O3 (2:3), KNO3 and Ca(NO3)2 with radicals, and Fe2O3, FeCl2 and CuO for elements with variable oxidation numbers.
lessons.learned: We learned that a radical is a charged group of atoms that stays together (NO3-, OH-, SO4 2-, CO3 2-, NH4+, PO4 3-), and that the criss-cross method, with brackets around radicals when a subscript is needed, helps us derive formulae by swapping valencies and checking that the total positive charge equals the total negative charge.
lessons.explained: We can explain that electron arrangement decides the ion charge (for example, the 1 outer electron of K gives K+, and 3 outer electrons of Al give Al3+). The ion charges then decide how many of each ion are needed to make a neutral compound, so we can predict formulae such as NaCl, CaCl2, Al2O3 and KNO3 and explain why Li, Na and K form similar compounds despite their different masses.

lessons.title: Writing and Balancing Chemical Equations: What Happens When Sodium Meets Water?
lessons.observed: We observed that sodium reacts with water by melting into a ball, darting and fizzing, that potassium reacts even more vigorously with a lilac flame and lithium more gently, that a gas (hydrogen) forms and the solution turns red litmus blue. We also saw that the unbalanced equation Na + H2O -> NaOH + H2 has unequal numbers of hydrogen atoms on each side.
lessons.learned: We learned that a chemical equation must have the same number of each kind of atom on both sides, and we balance it by changing coefficients only, never subscripts. We learned to use state symbols (s), (l), (g), (aq) and to write correct formulae first using valencies from Lesson 8.
lessons.explained: Li, Na and K have very different masses but each has one outer electron, so each loses it to form a 1+ ion and follows the same equation pattern, 2M + 2H2O -> 2MOH + H2 (for example 2Na + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + H2). The pattern is decided by the outer electron count, which sets the group, and not by mass. Balanced equations for 2Na + Cl2 -> 2NaCl, 4Al + 3O2 -> 2Al2O3 and Ca + 2HCl -> CaCl2 + H2 follow from the ions each element forms.
